title: Agent Mode
summary: Chat with an agent that reads, edits and runs commands in your workspace, following a workflow or as a single agent.

sections.text: **Agent Mode** is where most day-to-day work happens. Open it from the left rail. An agent can explore your code, edit files, run commands, search the web and ask you questions, within the permissions you set.

sections.heading: The message box
sections.text:
Type your request in the message box, which says **Message agent...**. A few things to know:

- Type `@` to reference a file, so the agent looks at exactly what you mean.
- Use **Add Context** to attach any file on disk to the prompt, or **Folder** to attach a folder.
- Choose a **skill** in the **Select skill** menu. New chats start with **build**. See [Skills](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/skills/). While the chat follows a workflow, the menu stays on **build** and reads *tools set per step*, because each step's profile decides its tools.
- Choose a **model** in the model picker. If you set up [automatic model selection](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/auto-model-selection/), **AUTO** appears here too. Reasoning-effort variants of a model are listed separately.

sections.heading: Workflow or single agent
sections.text:
Above the message box, the workflow bar's **Mode** menu picks how the chat runs:

| Choice | What happens |
|--------|--------------|
| **Single agent** | One agent loop decides its own path. Good for quick questions and small edits. New chats start here. |
| **Stage: …** (for example **Research & analyze**) | A short run, usually read-only, that stops at a written result for you to read. Run the next stage in the same chat and it builds on that result. |
| **Workflow: …** (for example **Plan, build, verify**, or one you made) | The chat follows it step by step from start to finish, pausing where a step needs your answer, such as approving the plan. |
| **Auto: choose a workflow for each message** | Rusty picks the workflow, or the single agent, for each message. Needs OpenRouter and a JEV model. |

When a workflow is selected, its name appears as a chip (click the **×** on it to stop following the workflow) and its steps are listed in order, for example *Request → Plan → Plan approval → Build → Verify → Acceptance → Manual checks → Result*. While it runs, the bar tells you where it is: *Running step 4 of 8: Build*, with *(waiting for permission)* when a step is blocked on a command prompt, *(waiting for your answer)* when an approval card is open above the message box, or the attempt number when a step is retrying. When a step fails, the bar marks it and shows the error, and your next message resumes the run there.

The **Allow flow switching** checkbox lets a running workflow hand over to another. **Auto mode** answers everything a run would ask you (see [below](#auto-mode)). The chevron at the left hides or shows the bar. See [When a workflow asks you](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/workflows/#when-a-workflow-asks-you).

The workflow's final message is its result, so read it: a finished run means every step finished, not that every check passed.

sections.heading: Auto mode
sections.text:
Tick **Auto mode** in the workflow bar (it is there with or without a workflow, and while a run goes on) and no run waits for you:

- commands, checks and file writes are allowed, each once, as if you had clicked **Allow once**;
- an approval step is approved: the plan as written, manual checks untried, and steps marked **Always ask a person** too;
- a stuck task is tried once more, then skipped; a run is never stopped for you;
- a question the agent asks takes its first suggestion, or the agent is told to decide itself and say in its answer what it chose.

It is one switch for every chat and is remembered across restarts. It works at once: turning it on also answers what is already waiting. A workflow step answered this way says so in the chat (*Plan approval: "Approve" was chosen by auto mode.*). Turn it on for long jobs you leave alone, such as a [goal](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/goals) with no `loops=` limit, and read the result afterwards.

Everything about workflows has its own section:

- [Workflows](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/workflows/): stages and pipelines, running one, answering its approvals, and steering a long job between stages.
- [How workflows work](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/how-workflows-work/): steps, handoffs, checks that send work back, approvals, task queues, subflows and limits.
- [Built-in workflows](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/built-in-workflows/): all 15, step by step.
- [Auto flows](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/auto-flows/): letting Rusty choose, and handing over mid-run.
- [Profiles & workflows](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/behaviors/): customizing them and the JSON behind them.

With **AUTO** selected in the model picker, each workflow step also picks its own model. See [Automatic model selection](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/auto-model-selection/#workflows-a-model-for-each-step).

sections.heading: What agents can do
sections.text:
Depending on the profile and permissions in force, an agent can use tools such as:

| Tool | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `read_file`, `list_files` | Read files and explore the workspace. `list_files` gives an overview with no arguments, lists a folder with `path` (and `depth` for more levels), or finds files by name with `glob`, such as `**/package.json`. Dependency and build-output folders are left out. With [smart file reading](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/smart-tools/) on, `read_file` returns only relevant sections. |
| `project_info` | Work out what kind of project the workspace holds and how to check it: languages and frameworks, the package manager, the install, typecheck, lint, test and build commands (from `package.json` scripts, Cargo, pyproject, `go.mod`, Makefile and your CI workflows), how to start dev servers, and whether dependencies are installed. Agents call it before running a build or test instead of guessing. Whatever allows `read_file` also allows it. A short summary of what it finds (the projects, which checks each has, and whether dependencies are missing) is also added to the agent's instructions when a chat starts, so it knows what it is working in from the first message. It is left out when the workspace takes more than a couple of seconds to scan, so it never holds up a chat. |
| `search_codebase` | Search your code. Also available as a ranked smart search. |
| `edit_file` | Change part of an existing file by replacing one exact piece of its text. It fails without touching the file if the text is missing or appears more than once. Whatever allows `write_file` also allows `edit_file`. |
| `write_file` | Create a new file, or replace a file's whole content. Replacing a file that already has content is refused unless the agent sets `overwrite: true`, so an accidental rewrite cannot silently drop code. |
| `run_check` | Run one of the project's own checks (`typecheck`, `lint`, `test`, `build` or `format`) and get a clear **PASSED** or **FAILED**. The commands come from `project_info`. A failure lists its errors as `file:line: message`, shows test counts, and says whether the cause is the code or the environment, for example dependencies that are not installed, in which case the agent installs them instead of editing code. A failing check is reported to the agent as a failed tool call. To run just one test while it works on it, the agent can give the `test` check a `test_name` or a `test_file` (for vitest, jest, pytest, `cargo test` and `go test`; other runners are refused, with a pointer to `run_command`). A filter that matches no test is reported as **FAILED**, never as a pass, because several runners exit successfully when nothing matched. The built-in Build, Refactor, Optimize and Verify profiles will not let an agent finish until it has run one (see [completion gates](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/behaviors/#completion-gates)). You approve each command as you would for `run_command`, and whatever allows `run_command` also allows `run_check`. |
| `install_dependencies` | Install the project's dependencies with its own package manager when `project_info` or a check says they are missing. It is not a check and never counts as having run one, so the agent runs the check again afterwards. Approved like `run_command`, and allowed wherever `run_command` is. |
| `run_command` | Run any other shell command, after you approve it. See [Permissions & safety](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/permissions/). |
| `web_search`, `web_extract`, `web_fetch` | Search the web and read pages. Needs a [search provider](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/smart-tools/#web-search-providers) for `web_search`. |
| `rusty_docs` | Look up Rusty's own documentation. See [Ask about Rusty](#ask-about-rusty). |
| `report_progress` | Tell you how the work is going. |
| `ask_user_question` | Ask you a question and wait for the answer. |

Agents can also delegate parts of a task to subagents.

sections.heading: Ask about Rusty
sections.text:
You can ask the agent about Rusty itself, in the same chat you use for your code. It looks the answer up in the documentation and replies with the steps, the exact name and place of each setting, and a link to the page it used. For example:

- How does spec-driven development work?
- Why do I have JEV, and what does it do?
- Where do I turn on smart file reading?

There is nothing to set up. Ask in a **Single agent** chat, which is how new chats start, with any skill. Steps of a workflow do not have this tool.

The documentation ships with the app, so answers match the version you have installed. Looking something up needs no internet connection, search provider or approval. Writing the answer is an ordinary request to your chosen model, so you need a [connected provider](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/providers/). If the documentation does not cover your question, the agent says so.

sections.heading: Permission prompts
sections.text: When an agent wants to run a command, Rusty shows **Command permission required** and waits. You can **Deny**, **Allow once**, or allow the program for the rest of the session. Details are in [Permissions & safety](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/permissions/).

sections.heading: Chat history
sections.text:
Each chat is saved automatically in your workspace, under `.rusty/chats/`. Use the controls at the top of Agent Mode:

- **New chat** starts a fresh conversation.
- **Show chat history** and **Hide history** toggle the list of past chats.
- **Refresh** reloads the list.
- **Delete chat** removes one.

sections.heading: Long chats
sections.text:
**A chat is one conversation.** Each message you send continues the same agent session, so the agent still has everything from earlier in the chat: what it said, and also the files it read, the commands it ran and their results. A follow-up such as *now fix what you found* works from the evidence, not from a recap. The context bar above the chat grows as the chat goes on.

A chat starts a fresh session, carrying the earlier messages over as text, when it can't continue the old one:

- you switched the model, the skill or the mode (such as Plan);
- the previous run failed or you stopped it;
- a workflow ran in the chat;
- the chat was reopened after Rusty restarted.

A model can only read so much at once, so Rusty shrinks a long chat before sending it:

- **In the session.** As the conversation fills the model's window, old tool results are cut to a short note first, then the oldest steps are dropped. A tool call always stays with its result.
- **Earlier messages carried into a fresh session.** Once they take about 40% of the model's context window, the oldest are left out and the model is told how many were omitted. The model's window comes from the provider's model list, or else from a catalogue of known models; if neither has it, nothing is left out.

The opening request is always kept word for word.

**Pinning a message.** Hover over a message and select the pin to keep it word for word however long the chat gets. A pinned message shows **Pinned**; select it again to unpin. Pins are saved with the chat. Many pinned messages can make a chat larger than its usual budget.

**Summaries.** Your chat's model also writes a running summary of what aged out, so it stands in for the messages that were left out. After a run, the older messages are folded into the summary, which is saved with the chat and used from the next run on. Within a run, older steps are summarized the same way. Summaries are written in the background, so no request waits for one, and if one fails the trimming above keeps the request in budget. Each summary is one extra call on your chat's provider, recorded in Token Metrics. Summaries are on by default; turn off **Summarize long conversations** in **Settings → Intelligence → Context compaction** to only trim.

**JEV ratings.** With OpenRouter and a JEV decision model connected, like [Automatic model selection](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/auto-model-selection/), turn on **Rate messages with JEV first (experimental)** in the same place. Before a summary, JEV rates the older messages: essential ones stay word for word, disposable ones are dropped, and only the rest is summarized. Each rated batch is one Decisions API request.

sections.heading: Reviewing what changed
sections.text:
Agents edit the real files in your workspace. Review their work in [Source control](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/source-control/): open each file's diff, stage what you want to keep, and commit.

> [!TIP]
> Give the agent a way to check its own work. Mention the test or type-check command in your request, or in the instructions of your Build profile, and the completion gate will hold the agent to it.

title: Appearance & shortcuts
summary: Themes, text sizes, large-file handling and keyboard shortcuts.

sections.text: Open **Settings** from the bottom of the left rail. It has four categories: **Appearance**, **Editor**, **Intelligence** and **System**. This page covers the first two. Intelligence is covered in [Automatic model selection](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/auto-model-selection/) and [Smart tools & web search](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/smart-tools/), and System in [Installation](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/installation/#updating) and [Troubleshooting](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/troubleshooting/).

sections.heading: Appearance
sections.text:
### Theme

Under **Appearance**, use the **Theme** menu to choose **Dark** or **Light**. The theme applies everywhere: the interface, the editor, the terminal, diffs and syntax colors.

### Text sizes

**Text sizes** has three independent controls, and each updates immediately:

| Control | Applies to |
|---------|-----------|
| **Editor text** | Code editors and diff editors. |
| **Chat text** | Messages, Markdown, activity and the composer. |
| **Interface text** | The sidebar, tabs, toolbars, panels and dialogs. |

A live preview underneath shows the effect.

sections.heading: Editor
sections.text:
### Large file handling

Very large files can make an editor slow. Under **Large file handling**, the **Large-file threshold** sets the size above which a file opens **read-only, with the language server disabled**, instead of the normal editable path. The threshold is in megabytes: it defaults to 5 MB and can be set from 1 MB to 50 MB. **Reset** restores the default.

Binary files always get an unsupported-file preview instead, whatever their size.

sections.heading: Keyboard shortcuts
sections.text:
**Settings → Editor → Keyboard shortcuts** shows the shortcuts Rusty uses. The defaults are:

| Action | Shortcut |
|--------|----------|
| Close active tab | <kbd>⌘</kbd> <kbd>W</kbd> |
| Open search | <kbd>⌘</kbd> <kbd>K</kbd> |
| Toggle explorer | <kbd>⌘</kbd> <kbd>1</kbd> |

Other shortcuts you will use:

| Where | Shortcut | Action |
|-------|----------|--------|
| Editor | <kbd>⌘</kbd> <kbd>Enter</kbd> | Open [Inline Chat](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/inline-chat/) on the current selection or line. |
| Inline Chat | <kbd>Enter</kbd> | Send. |
| Inline Chat | <kbd>Shift</kbd> <kbd>Enter</kbd> | New line. |
| Inline Chat | <kbd>Esc</kbd> | Close. |
| Source Control | <kbd>⌘</kbd> <kbd>Enter</kbd> | Commit, from the commit message box. |

The search palette opened with <kbd>⌘</kbd> <kbd>K</kbd> searches the workspace.

title: Auto flows
summary: Let Rusty choose the workflow for each message, and hand a running workflow over to another when what it finds changes the plan.

sections.text:
[Workflows](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/workflows/) are most useful when the right one is running. **Auto flows** make that Rusty's job. There are two parts:

- **Auto** chooses the workflow, or the single agent, for each message.
- **Allow flow switching** lets a running workflow hand over to another when what a step found changes the plan.

Both use the same decision model (JEV) as [automatic model selection](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/auto-model-selection/), and both are on the record in [observability](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/observability/).

> [!NOTE]
> Auto flows need **OpenRouter** connected and a **JEV decision model** chosen, like automatic model selection. Without them the **Auto** entry does not appear in the Mode menu. A saved Auto chat still shows it, labelled *Auto (needs OpenRouter and a JEV model)*, and answers with the single agent. See [Automatic model selection](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/auto-model-selection/#set-it-up).

sections.heading: Let Rusty choose the workflow (Auto)
sections.text:
Open the **Mode** menu in the workflow bar and choose **Auto: choose a workflow for each message**. From then on, Rusty decides for every message whether to answer directly or follow a workflow.

It chooses between **Single agent**, the read-only stages (**Research & analyze**, **Architect & plan**, **Debug & plan a fix**, **Security audit & fix plan** and **Verify & review changes**) and **Build & verify**. It looks at your message, what you asked earlier in the chat, an excerpt of the last result, and how the previous workflow ended. So after a Research & analyze run, "design it" goes to **Architect & plan** and builds on that result.

| What Rusty finds | What happens |
|------------------|--------------|
| A confident pick that cannot change files | It starts straight away and says what it chose, for example *↳ AUTO · Stage: Research & analyze (88% confidence)*. |
| A confident pick that can change files (Build & verify) | It starts straight away too, and says so: *↳ AUTO · Stage: Build & verify (90% confidence) · can change files*. It still shows you its plan to approve before it builds, and its tool permissions, such as approving a command, still apply. |
| It is not sure | The **Single agent** answers, and the chat says *↳ AUTO · Single agent (no workflow was a clear fit)*. |
| The decision service cannot be reached | It answers with the single agent and says why. A message is never blocked. |

Auto never starts an [end-to-end pipeline](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/built-in-workflows/#pipelines) by itself: choose one from the Mode menu. Which workflows Auto may pick is decided by whether a workflow has a [`metadata.route.when`](#opt-your-own-workflows-in) description.

What counts as "can change files" is read from the profiles a workflow's steps use, so it holds for workflows you write too.

While a chat is on Auto, the **skill** menu is locked to **build** only while a workflow it chose is running. Between messages, and when Rusty answers with the single agent, your chosen skill applies as usual. A failed run resumes only if Auto chooses the same workflow for your next message; otherwise Rusty starts fresh.

sections.heading: Hand over mid-run
sections.text:
Sometimes a run shows it should be a different flow: a Plan step finds the request is really a bug, or Verify finds a security problem. Turn on **Allow flow switching** in the workflow bar and Rusty can hand the run over.

The setting is **per chat**, **off by default**, and saved with the chat. It appears once a workflow or Auto is selected, and works for a workflow you picked yourself as well as for Auto. A workflow that lists workflows it may hand over to (see [below](#opt-your-own-workflows-in)) is affected; the built-in workflows all list some.

With it on, the workflow is **held after each step that has another step following it**. The step finishes first. The next step waits while Rusty checks whether what was found means another workflow is the right one. The status line reads *Checking whether to switch flows…*.

- **Usually it carries on.** Anything short of a confident pick of another workflow continues as planned, and so does any failure of the check.
- **A confident pick hands over.** The run ends, keeping what finished, and the next workflow starts in the same turn. It receives your request plus the outputs of the finished steps as context. The chat shows *↪ AUTO · Handing over to Stage: Debug & plan a fix (86% confidence)*, and the bar swaps to the new workflow's steps.
- **Handing over never asks you.** If the workflow it hands over to can change files, the chat says so: *↪ AUTO · Handing over to … It can change files.* The built-in workflows only hand over to read-only stages. A run that hands over saves no report, because the next run continues from its work, which is already in the conversation.

A chat that followed one workflow now follows the one it handed over to, and keeps it for your next message. An Auto chat stays on Auto.

### Limits

- At most **two hand-overs** happen per message.
- A workflow already run in the turn is never run again, so a hand-over cannot loop.
- **Stop** ends the whole turn, including a check that is still pending.
- Each workflow in a chain has its own budgets and limits.
- Every check costs one decision-model request, and only workflows with something to hand over to make one.

sections.heading: What is sent to the decision model
sections.text:
Choosing and handing over each send a short prompt to the **OpenRouter Decisions API**, using your OpenRouter key and your chosen JEV model. They are not sent to the provider of the model that does your work.

| Decision | What it sees |
|----------|--------------|
| **Choosing a workflow** | Your message (up to 4,000 characters), an excerpt of the last result (up to 2,000 characters), the name and outcome of the previous workflow run, and a one-line description of each workflow it may pick. |
| **Handing over** | The request the workflow was started with (up to 4,000 characters), the outputs of the steps finished so far (up to 3,000 characters each and 9,000 in total, latest first), the names of the steps still to run, and a description of each workflow it may hand over to. |

No files are read for these decisions. Choosing a workflow sees only what you typed, not your attachments. A hand-over check sees the request as the workflow received it, which includes any attached file context, within that 4,000-character limit, and the step outputs, which can quote your code. If the decision service takes longer than about 10 seconds, Rusty carries on without it.

sections.heading: Opt your own workflows in
sections.text:
Two optional fields in a workflow's `metadata` connect it to Auto and to flow switching. The built-in workflows set them; yours can too.

```json
"metadata": {
  "route": { "when": "The user wants to understand how existing functionality works before deciding anything." },
  "switch_to": ["diagnose", "security-audit"]
}
```

`route.when` describes when the workflow is the right one for a message, and a workflow without it is never picked by Auto. `switch_to` lists the workflows this one may hand over to, and a workflow without it never hands over. Write `when` as a description of the **situation**, not of the steps: "Something is broken and the user wants the cause found" routes better than "Runs Debug and Plan". The full format is in [Choosing and switching flows](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/behaviors/#choosing-and-switching-flows).

sections.heading: Confidence
sections.text: The confidence needed to act on a pick follows **Act on JEV's pick at confidence** under **Settings → Intelligence** (60% or higher by default), the same setting JEV decisions use. Below it, Auto answers with the single agent and a running workflow carries on.

sections.heading: See what it decided
sections.text: Each decision is recorded in [Tool Execution Observability](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/observability/#flow-decisions) as **AUTO flow selection** or **AUTO flow switching**, with the request, the probabilities, the confidence and what the decision cost.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text:
**The Auto entry is missing.** Connect OpenRouter, refresh its model catalog and choose a JEV decision model. See [Automatic model selection](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/auto-model-selection/#set-it-up).

**It asks me to approve a plan.** That is **Build & verify**, or a pipeline you chose, showing you its plan before it changes anything. Choosing a workflow never asks, whether or not it can change files. Approve the plan, or tick **Auto mode** in the workflow bar so that nothing waits for you. See [When a workflow asks you](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/workflows/#when-a-workflow-asks-you).

**It answers with the single agent when I expected a workflow.** No workflow was a clear fit at the confidence setting. Lower the setting if you are comfortable with that, or choose the workflow yourself.

**The message says *Could not choose a workflow*.** The decision service could not be reached or answered with an error, so Rusty answered with the single agent. The reason follows in the message.

**A workflow never hands over.** Check that **Allow flow switching** is on, that the workflow lists workflows it may hand over to, that the step that just finished is not the last one, and that you have not already used both hand-overs this message. The check carries on unless it is confident, so it is normal for most runs to finish where they started.

**A stage did not build on the last result.** The context is the last assistant result in the chat. A new chat starts clean. Every built-in workflow reads it; a workflow of your own reads it only if one of its steps binds `/context`.

title: Automatic model selection
summary: Let Rusty rate each request and route it to the model you chose for Light, Standard or Heavy work.

sections.text: Automatic model selection adds **AUTO** to the Agent model picker. Instead of choosing a model for every message, you assign a model to each of three levels once. Rusty rates each request and runs it on the model for that level, so quick questions stay fast and cheap while hard problems get a stronger model.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text:
1. You choose **AUTO** in the Agent model picker.
2. A decision model, called **JEV** in the app, rates the request as **Light**, **Standard** or **Heavy**. It never sees your model list, so your mapping alone decides what runs.
3. The model you assigned to that level runs the request.

When the decision model is unsure and leans toward a higher level, AUTO steps up one level. Under-powering a request costs more than over-paying for it.

| Level | Typical requests |
|-------|------------------|
| **Light** | Conversation, factual questions, explaining code, and small single-file edits. |
| **Standard** | Features and bug fixes across a few files, tests, reviews, and debugging with a clear error. |
| **Heavy** | Architecture, large refactors, subtle concurrency or performance bugs, and long multi-step tasks. |

sections.heading: Workflows: a model for each step
sections.text:
A workflow's steps differ a lot in difficulty. Research and Verify read and report, while Architect and Debug reason hard, so rating the whole message once would waste a strong model or starve a hard step. When **AUTO** is selected and the chat follows a [workflow](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/built-in-workflows/), the choice is made per step instead:

1. The run starts on your **Standard** model. Rusty does not rate the message up front.
2. Just before each agent step's first model turn, JEV rates **that step** as Light, Standard or Heavy. It sees the step's instructions, your request and the hand-offs from earlier steps, and the step runs on the model for that level.
3. Every turn of the step then uses that model. The next step is rated on its own.

The chat shows each choice, for example *↳ AUTO · Light task · your-model (90% confidence)*. As with single requests, an unsure rating steps up one level.

Some limits to know:

- A step can only switch to a model on the **same provider** the run started on. If a level's model is on another provider, or on a managed-login provider, that level is skipped and the nearest level on the same provider is used. Assign all three levels on one provider to get the full range.
- If the decision service is slow (over about 12 seconds) or fails, the step simply keeps your Standard model. Choosing never stops a step.
- Each rating costs one Decisions API request.

sections.heading: Set it up
sections.text:
**Requirements:** an OpenRouter API key, and a **JEV Decisions API** model available in your OpenRouter model book.

1. Connect **OpenRouter** in **LLM Integrations** with your API key. See [Model providers](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/providers/).
2. Refresh the OpenRouter model catalog so the decision models appear.
3. Open **Settings → Intelligence → Intelligent model selection**.
4. Under **JEV decision model**, choose a version. All compatible versions from your authenticated OpenRouter model book are listed.
5. Assign a model to each of the three levels. You can use any model from any connected provider, reasoning-effort variants included.
6. Turn on **Enabled**.

The panel shows a status line. **Ready** means AUTO is available. If it is not, the message tells you what is missing: connect OpenRouter, refresh the model book, or choose a model for a specific level.

> [!TIP]
> Start with a fast model for Light, a balanced one for Standard and your strongest model for Heavy. Adjust after you see how the decisions play out.

sections.heading: See what it decided
sections.text: Every AUTO decision is recorded in Tool Execution Observability, including the request, the probabilities for each level, the confidence, the model chosen and what the decision cost. In a workflow, each step's decision is recorded separately as **AUTO model selection · *step***. See [Observability & metrics](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/observability/).

sections.heading: Related: choosing the workflow
sections.text: The same decision model can also choose the **workflow** for a message, and hand a running workflow over to another. That is separate from choosing a model, and the two combine: Auto picks the workflow, then **AUTO** picks a model for each of its steps. See [Let Rusty choose the workflow](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/auto-flows/). Each routing decision is recorded in Tool Execution Observability as **AUTO flow selection** or **AUTO flow switching**.

sections.heading: Related experimental features
sections.text:
The same decision model powers four experimental features, also under **Settings → Intelligence**:

- **JEV decisions (experimental).** Agents lay out options and JEV picks one. In AUTO chats it can also move a chat up to a stronger model when the remaining work needs it. A setting controls the confidence at which Rusty acts on JEV's pick.
- **JEV review of risky actions (experimental).** Before an agent overwrites a file destructively or runs a destructive command, JEV reviews the step. It can let it run, send the agent back to revise, or ask you.
- **JEV decision review (experimental).** A shadow mode that scores every tool call any model makes as Proceed, Revise or Stop. The call always runs and the verdict is only recorded in [Tool Execution Observability](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/observability/#jev-decision-review). Each scored call is one Decisions API request.
- **JEV ratings for summaries (experimental).** When a chat grows long, JEV rates which older messages and run steps still matter before they are summarized. Essential ones stay word for word, disposable ones are dropped, and your chat's model summarizes the rest in the background. See [Long chats](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/agent-mode/#long-chats).

All four need OpenRouter connected with a decision model chosen, and all may change between releases.

title: Profiles & workflows
summary: Design how agents work in the Behaviors editor, and understand the plain JSON files behind it.

sections.text:
A single agent loop decides its own path. A **workflow** decides it for the agent: which steps run, what each may use, what must be verified, and what happens on failure. Each agent step runs under a **profile** that sets its instructions, tools, limits and completion checks.

Both are edited in the **Behaviors** tab and stored as plain JSON in your workspace:

| Kind | Location |
|------|----------|
| Profiles | `.rusty/profiles/<id>.json` |
| Workflows | `.rusty/workflows/<id>.json` |

> [!NOTE]
> Rusty ships with [12 profiles and 20 workflows](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/built-in-workflows/), available in every project. Choose one from the **Mode** menu in Agent Mode. They are read-only, so they always stay in a known-good state. To change one, choose **Customize a copy**: you get your own editable copy, saved in your workspace. This page is about customizing and writing your own. To learn what the built-in ones do and how to run them, start with [Workflows](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/workflows/).

sections.heading: The Behaviors editor
sections.text:
> [!TIP]
> Every control is described in [The workflow editor](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/workflow-editor/), and [Your first workflow](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/first-workflow/) walks through making one. This section is a short summary.

Open **Behaviors** in the left rail. A switch at the top left toggles between **Workflows** and **Profiles**, and the list beside it shows what you have. The built-in workflows and profiles are tagged **Built-in**.

- The **workflow** view draws steps as nodes and their connections as edges. The buttons above the canvas add steps: **Input**, **Agent**, **Verify**, **Approval**, **Subflow** and **Output**. Select a step or an edge to edit it in the inspector, drag from a step's right handle to another step to connect them, and drill into an agent step to see its profile.
- The **profile** view draws profiles as nodes, with `switch_profile` rules drawn as edges between them.
- Steps show the state of the latest run, such as *succeeded* or *running*, and a badge such as *Last run cancelled* summarizes it.
- **Run in Agent Mode** starts the selected workflow from Agent Mode, with that chat's model and tools. **New workflow** creates one.
- Edits are validated as you make them, and a step or profile with a validation problem is flagged.
- A dot marks unsaved changes, and the button at the top right reads **Saved** when everything is written.

For a built-in workflow the inspector is read-only and says *Built into Rusty · available in every project*, with **Customize a copy** at the top.

### The workflow inspector

With nothing selected, the inspector at the right edits the workflow itself:

| Field | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| **Name** and **Description** | How the workflow is listed and described. |
| **Revision** | A number you can bump as you change it. |
| **Status** | **Draft**, **Published** or **Deprecated**. |
| **Optional limits** | Budgets for a whole run. Leave a field empty for no limit. |

The optional limits are **Steps**, **Total attempts**, **Duration (seconds)**, **Stall timeout (seconds)**, **Model requests**, **Tool calls**, **Tokens** and **Cost (USD)**. You can also stop a running workflow at any time.

Because the documents are plain JSON, fields the editor does not know about survive a load and save. Use the JSON toggle in the inspector header to see and edit a document's raw JSON. Canvas positions are stored under `metadata.editor.position`, which the engine ignores.

sections.heading: Run a workflow
sections.text:
In **Agent Mode**, the **Mode** menu above the message box picks what the chat follows: **Single agent**, a **Stage**, a **Workflow**, or **Auto**. See [Workflows](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/workflows/) for how to run one and how stages build on each other, and [Auto flows](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/auto-flows/) for letting Rusty choose.

While a chat follows a workflow, the **skill** menu stays on **build** and reads *tools set per step*: each step's profile decides its tools.

sections.heading: Built-in profiles and workflows
sections.text: The 12 built-in profiles (Research, Analyze, Plan, Architect, Debug, Build, Verify, Review, Security, Document, Refactor and Optimize) and 15 built-in workflows are described in [Built-in workflows](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/built-in-workflows/), including what each step can do. Their IDs start with `rusty-ide.builtin.`. Customize a copy to start from any of them.

sections.heading: Profiles
sections.text:
A profile describes what one agent step may do. This is the built-in **Plan** profile, trimmed. (In the app its ID is `rusty-ide.builtin.plan`; your own profiles use the IDs you give them.)

```json
{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "id": "plan",
  "revision": 3,
  "name": "Plan",
  "description": "Read-only investigation. Explores the workspace and produces a concrete plan.",
  "status": "draft",
  "instructions": {
    "mode": "append",
    "text": "Investigate the request and write an actionable implementation plan..."
  },
  "tools": {
    "type": "allow_list",
    "tools": ["read_file", "list_files", "search_codebase", "web_search", "web_extract", "report_progress", "ask_user_question"]
  },
  "rules": [
    {
      "id": "plan-read-only",
      "on": "PreToolUse",
      "when": { "tool": ["write_file", "run_command"] },
      "do": { "deny": { "reason": "The plan step is read-only. Describe the change in the plan instead of making it." } }
    }
  ],
  "completion_gate": {
    "checks": [
      {
        "id": "explored-first",
        "require": { "calls": { "tool": ["read_file", "list_files", "search_codebase"], "gte": 1 } },
        "feedback": "You have not looked at the code yet. Explore the relevant files before proposing a plan."
      }
    ],
    "max_continuations": 2,
    "on_exhausted": "fail"
  }
}
```

### Profile fields

| Field | What it does |
|-------|--------------|
| `id`, `name`, `description`, `revision`, `status` | Identity and bookkeeping. Built-in profiles have IDs starting with `rusty-ide.builtin.`. |
| `instructions` | Text added to the agent's instructions. `mode: "append"` adds to the base instructions. |
| `tools` | Which tools the step may use. `{ "type": "inherit" }` keeps whatever the surrounding session allows. `{ "type": "allow_list", "tools": [...] }` limits it to the named tools. Anything written for `write_file` (an allow-list entry, a rule, a permission) also applies to `edit_file`, so a read-only profile stays read-only. Naming `edit_file` applies to that tool alone. An allow-list that names `read_file` also admits `project_info`, but a rule about `read_file` does not apply to it. Anything written for `run_command` (an allow-list entry, a rule, a permission, a gate that counts commands) also applies to `run_check` and `install_dependencies`, so a profile that forbids running commands forbids running checks and installs. Naming `run_check` itself matches only that tool, which is how a rule asks for a check in particular. |
| `tool_overrides` | Adjusts how a tool is described to the model, for example `description_append` to add a guideline to `write_file`. A description note applies to the named tool only: add one for `edit_file` separately if you want it there too. |
| `limits` | Optional turn and tool-call limits. Unset in the built-in flow. |
| `rules` | Event-driven rules that steer the agent. See below. |
| `completion_gate` | Checks the agent must satisfy before it is allowed to finish. See below. |
| `children` | Settings for subagents this step starts. `{ "type": "inherit" }` is the default. |

### Rules

A rule reacts to an event and takes an action.

```json
{
  "id": "build-failed-tool",
  "on": "PostToolUseFailure",
  "do": { "inject": { "text": "That tool call failed. Read the error and fix the cause; do not repeat the same call unchanged." } },
  "max_fires": 8
}
```

| Part | Values |
|------|--------|
| `on` (event) | `RunStart`, `BeforeModelRequest`, `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `PostToolUseFailure`, `ProfileEntered` |
| `when` (optional filter) | For example `{ "tool": ["write_file"] }` to match specific tools, or `{ "turn": { "gte": 3 } }` to match after a number of turns. |
| `do` (action) | `inject`, `deny`, `ask`, `allow`, `stop_run`, `switch_profile`, `rewrite_args`, `rewrite_result` |
| `max_fires` | Optional cap on how many times the rule can trigger. |

Which actions are valid depends on the event:

| Action | Effect | Valid on |
|--------|--------|----------|
| `inject` | Adds guidance text to the conversation. | Any event |
| `deny` | Blocks the tool call, with a reason the agent sees. | `PreToolUse` |
| `ask` | Asks you first. | `PreToolUse` |
| `allow` | Allows the call to proceed. | `PreToolUse` |
| `rewrite_args` | Merges values into the call's arguments. | `PreToolUse` |
| `rewrite_result` | Edits a tool's result before the agent sees it. | `PostToolUse`, `PostToolUseFailure` |
| `stop_run` | Ends the run, with a reason. | Any event |
| `switch_profile` | Hands the run to another profile. | Any event except `ProfileEntered` |

### Completion gates

A completion gate stops an agent from declaring victory too early. Each check has a `require` condition and a `feedback` message the agent receives when the check fails. The agent is sent back to keep working up to `max_continuations` times; if it still fails, `on_exhausted: "fail"` fails the step.

The built-in **Build** profile uses this to require that any edit is followed by a check:

```json
{
  "id": "checked-after-editing",
  "require": {
    "any": [
      { "calls": { "tool": "write_file", "eq": 0 } },
      { "since_last_call": { "of": "write_file", "called": "run_check", "gte": 1 } },
      { "all": [
        { "not": { "tool_offered": "run_check" } },
        { "since_last_call": { "of": "write_file", "called": ["run_command", "read_file"], "gte": 1 } }
      ] }
    ]
  },
  "feedback": "You changed files but have not run a check since your last edit. Call run_check (typecheck, lint, test or build) now; reading the changed file back does not count. If a check fails because of your change, fix it and run it again."
}
```

In words: either no files were written, or since the last write the agent ran `run_check`. Reading the file back does not count. If the session gave the agent no way to run a check at all (`tool_offered` is false for `run_check`), the older rule applies instead, so the gate can always be met. **Refactor** and **Optimize** work the same way, and **Verify** requires a `run_check` too, since reading files is not verification. `install_dependencies` is a separate tool from `run_check` on purpose: installing proves nothing about the code, so it can never stand in for having run a check.

A check that ran and **failed** still satisfies this gate. It asks that the agent looked, not that the project is green, because a project that was already failing before the agent touched it could otherwise never finish. What happens after a failure is handled by a rule instead: while a check has failed since the last edit and none has passed, the agent is reminded to fix what it broke, or to name failures that were already there, and never to call the work passing.

**Build must finish what it was given.** Build ends its report with a status line, `Status: done` or `Status: blocked — <what only you can provide>`, and its gate has a `work-finished` check that requires one of them: `{ "final_status": ["done", "complete", "completed", "blocked*"] }`. A report that says `Status: not done`, or has no status, is sent back with "continue with the next unfinished task" instead of going on to Verify half done. `final_status` reads the last `Status:` line (or the line under a `## Status` heading, or the `status` field of a JSON answer), lower-cased and cut at the first dash or punctuation, so `**Status:** Not done — tests remain` reads as `not done`. The check is marked `"waive_when_exhausted": true`: when the gate runs out of `max_continuations`, it lets the answer through (Verify still judges the work) rather than failing the step, while any other failing check still applies `on_exhausted`.

Conditions can look at whether a call succeeded or failed. `outcome` (`succeeded` or `failed`) narrows `calls`, `turns_since_call` and the `called` side of `since_last_call` to calls whose result was or was not an error, and `run_check` reports a failing check as an error. To require a *passing* check, use `"called": "run_check", "outcome": "succeeded"` in your own copy of a profile. That suits a project whose checks are green. A command run through `run_command` always counts as succeeded, because the harness cannot read a failure out of its output; that is one reason to prefer `run_check`.

sections.heading: Workflows
sections.text:
A workflow is a graph of steps. For the ideas behind it (what each kind of step does, how work is handed on and sent back), read [How workflows work](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/how-workflows-work/) first. This is a minimal plan, build and verify flow with text handoffs:

```json
{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "id": "plan-build-verify",
  "name": "Plan, build, verify",
  "status": "draft",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "input", "name": "Request", "type": "input" },
    {
      "id": "plan", "name": "Plan", "type": "agent",
      "config": {
        "instructions": "Investigate the request and write an actionable implementation plan...",
        "tools": { "type": "inherit" },
        "context_mode": "isolated_child",
        "structured_output": "text",
        "profile": { "id": "plan" }
      },
      "input_bindings": [
        { "target": "request", "source": { "type": "run_input", "pointer": "/request" } }
      ]
    },
    {
      "id": "build", "name": "Build", "type": "agent",
      "config": { "context_mode": "isolated_child", "structured_output": "text", "profile": { "id": "build" } },
      "input_bindings": [
        { "target": "request", "source": { "type": "run_input", "pointer": "/request" } },
        { "target": "plan", "source": { "type": "node_output", "node_id": "plan", "pointer": "" } }
      ]
    },
    {
      "id": "verify", "name": "Verify", "type": "agent",
      "config": { "context_mode": "isolated_child", "structured_output": "text", "profile": { "id": "verify" } },
      "input_bindings": [
        { "target": "request", "source": { "type": "run_input", "pointer": "/request" } },
        { "target": "plan", "source": { "type": "node_output", "node_id": "plan", "pointer": "" } },
        { "target": "build", "source": { "type": "node_output", "node_id": "build", "pointer": "" } }
      ]
    },
    {
      "id": "output", "name": "Result", "type": "output",
      "config": { "source": { "type": "node_output", "node_id": "verify", "pointer": "" } }
    }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "id": "input-plan", "source": "input", "target": "plan", "condition": "on_success" },
    { "id": "plan-build", "source": "plan", "target": "build", "condition": "on_success" },
    { "id": "build-verify", "source": "build", "target": "verify", "condition": "on_success" },
    { "id": "verify-output", "source": "verify", "target": "output", "condition": "on_success" }
  ]
}
```

### Steps

| Step `type` | Purpose |
|-------------|---------|
| `input` | Receives the run input (`request`, `context`, `attachments`). Exactly one per workflow. |
| `agent` | Runs an agent, optionally under a `profile`, and optionally as a `task_queue`. |
| `verify` | Checks earlier results without a model. A failure sends the work back to its `retry_target`, follows an `on_failure` edge, or fails the run. |
| `approval` | Waits for a person to approve, request changes (sent back to `revise_target`) or reject. |
| `subflow` | Runs a saved workflow, or one step, inside this one. |
| `output` | Picks which step's output becomes the workflow's result. At least one, and nothing may follow it. |

Every agent step runs in a fresh, isolated session (`context_mode: "isolated_child"`) that inherits your workspace, active model and permission policies. Steps hand work to each other as ordinary text or Markdown unless a step sets a JSON `structured_output` with an `output_schema`. A finished workflow means every step finished, not that every check passed, so read the result.

### Inputs and edges

- `input_bindings` say where each named input to a step comes from: the run input (`{"type": "run_input", "pointer": "/request"}`) or an earlier step's output (`{"type": "node_output", "node_id": "plan", "pointer": ""}`). `pointer` is a JSON pointer: `""` is the whole value, `/summary` one field. The `target` is the name the agent sees in its `workflow_input`. A step can read only steps that are certain to have run before it.
- `edges` connect steps. `condition` is `on_success` for the normal path or `on_failure` to route a failure somewhere else. Each step has exactly one `on_success` edge (output steps none) and at most one `on_failure` edge. Cycles are refused: loops come from `retry_target` and `revise_target`.
- `retry` on a step sets `max_attempts` (1 to 10) and `retry_on`, the failures that may use them: `backend_rate_limited`, `backend_timeout`, `tool_timeout`, `invalid_structured_output` and `verification_failed`. A step that a verify step retries must list `verification_failed`.

### Verify steps and checks

```json
{
  "id": "gate", "name": "Acceptance", "type": "verify",
  "config": {
    "checks": [{ "type": "criteria", "pointer": "/check/criteria", "plan_pointer": "/plan" }],
    "retry_target": "build"
  },
  "input_bindings": [
    { "target": "check", "source": { "type": "node_output", "node_id": "verify", "pointer": "" } },
    { "target": "plan", "source": { "type": "node_output", "node_id": "plan", "pointer": "" } }
  ]
}
```

Pointers in checks read the step's bound inputs, by binding name.

| Check | Fields | Passes when |
|-------|--------|-------------|
| `criteria` | `pointer`; optional `plan_pointer`, `block_on` (default `["fail"]`), `defer` (default `["manual"]`), `max_deferred` | The `{id, status, evidence, how_to_test?}` list at `pointer` is not empty and has no `block_on` status. A `defer` status moves on and is collected in the step's `manual_checks`. With `plan_pointer`, every acceptance criterion of that plan must be reported. |
| `required_status` | `pointer`, `equals` | The text at `pointer` equals `equals`. |
| `artifact_exists` | `pointer` | The value at `pointer` is present and not empty. |
| `artifacts_resolvable` | `pointer` | Every `{kind, reference}` entry in the list at `pointer` resolves in the workspace. |
| `schema` | none | Every bound output matches its producer's `output_schema`. |
| `requirements_satisfied` | `plan_pointer`, `results_pointer` | Every acceptance criterion in the plan has exactly one passing, evidenced result. |

`retry_target` names an earlier agent step to send failed work back to, with the failure as feedback. The steps between run again. Without it, a failure follows the step's `on_failure` edge or fails the run.

### Approval steps

The two approvals in the built-in pipelines:

```json
{
  "id": "approve_plan", "name": "Plan approval", "type": "approval",
  "config": {
    "subject": { "type": "node_output", "node_id": "plan", "pointer": "" },
    "prompt": "Read the plan before anything is built. ...",
    "revise_on_notes": true
  }
},
{
  "id": "confirm_checks", "name": "Manual checks", "type": "approval",
  "config": {
    "subject": { "type": "node_output", "node_id": "gate", "pointer": "/manual_checks" },
    "prompt": "Verification passed, but these checks need a person. ...",
    "revise_target": "build",
    "skip_if_empty": ""
  }
}
```

| Field | Default | Meaning |
|-------|---------|---------|
| `subject` | required | What the person reviews: a run-input or step-output binding. |
| `prompt` | generic question | Shown above the subject. |
| `revise_target` | the subject's step | The earlier agent step that requested changes go back to. |
| `max_revisions` | `5` | How often changes may be requested (at most 10). Requested changes do not use the target's attempts. |
| `allow_auto_approve` | `true` | Whether the run may pass this step by itself. `false` asks, unless **Auto mode** is on, which approves it too. |
| `skip_if_empty` | never skip | A pointer into the subject; when nothing is there, the step passes without asking. `""` means the subject itself. |
| `revise_on_notes` | `false` | Approving with notes revises the result first, then the approval stands. |

The step's output is `{decision, by, notes, subject}`, so a later step can read the person's notes, as the built-ins do with `{"type": "node_output", "node_id": "approve_plan", "pointer": "/notes"}`.

### Subflow steps

```json
{
  "id": "investigate", "name": "Investigate", "type": "subflow",
  "config": { "target": { "type": "flow", "id": "rusty-ide.builtin.investigate" } },
  "input_bindings": [
    { "target": "request", "source": { "type": "run_input", "pointer": "/request" } },
    { "target": "context", "source": { "type": "run_input", "pointer": "/context" } }
  ]
}
```

`target` is either `{"type": "flow", "id": "...", "revision": 2}` (`revision` optional; the latest otherwise) or `{"type": "step", "instructions": "...", "profile": {"id": "..."}, "tools": {...}, "model": "..."}`, where only `instructions` is required. The step's bindings are the child run's input, and the child's result is the step's output. Flows can call flows three levels deep. Saved workflows that a run calls are sent with it, and the built-in ones are always available.

### Task queues

An agent step with `task_queue` builds a plan task by task:

```json
"task_queue": {
  "plan_pointer": "/plan",
  "review_profile": { "id": "rusty-ide.builtin.review" },
  "review_instructions": "Review the change made for workflow_input.task against its acceptance criteria. ...",
  "max_repairs": 2,
  "on_task_failure": "ask"
}
```

`plan_pointer` points into the step's bound inputs: its first segment names the binding the plan comes from, and that plan must contain requirements with acceptance criteria and tasks (the built-ins give Plan the `rusty.task_plan` output schema). `on_task_failure` is `ask`, `skip` or `stop`. An optional `flows` map, `{"research": {"type": "flow", "id": "..."}}`, names workflows a task may run instead of a builder by setting its `flow`. The step's output is an object listing the completed tasks, whatever its response format.

### Limits and timeouts

`policies` holds the workflow's budgets, all optional: `max_steps`, `max_total_attempts`, `max_elapsed_ms`, `stall_timeout_ms`, `max_model_requests`, `max_tool_calls`, `max_tokens` and `max_cost_usd`. The built-in workflows set `max_total_attempts` to 40 and `stall_timeout_ms` to 600000 (10 minutes without a sign of life cancels and retries a step; waiting for a person does not count). A step can also set `timeout_ms`, and a profile `limits` (turns and tool calls); the built-in profiles leave those unset. The editor offers fields for all of them, and workflows written as raw JSON keep working through the advanced settings.

sections.heading: Choosing and switching flows
sections.text:
Two optional fields in a workflow's `metadata` (which the engine ignores) let [Auto and flow switching](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/auto-flows/) work with it. The built-in workflows set them; your own can too.

```json
"metadata": {
  "route": { "when": "The user wants to understand how existing functionality works before deciding anything." },
  "switch_to": ["diagnose", "security-audit"]
}
```

| Field | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `route.when` | When this workflow is the right one for a message, in a sentence or two. The decision model reads it. A workflow without it is never picked by Auto. |
| `switch_to` | Ids of the workflows this one may hand over to when flow switching is on. Use the workflow's `id`; for a built-in workflow, the id without `rusty-ide.builtin.`. A workflow without it never hands over. |

Whether a workflow **can change files** is not declared: Rusty reads it from the profiles its steps use. A workflow edits unless every agent step's profile either has an allow-list without `write_file`, or has a `PreToolUse` rule that denies `write_file`. Auto and flow switching ask before starting one that does.

The built-in workflows hand over only to the read-only stages. For example Plan, build, verify may hand over to **Research & analyze**, **Debug & plan a fix** or **Security audit & fix plan**.

sections.heading: Tips
sections.text:
> [!TIP]
> Start from **Customize a copy** of the built-in flow rather than writing from scratch. Change a profile's instructions, add a `deny` rule for a command you never want run, or tighten the tool allow-list, and watch how the next run behaves.

- Commit `.rusty/profiles/` and `.rusty/workflows/` so your team shares the same behavior.
- Keep completion-gate feedback specific. It is the message the agent acts on.
- Use `deny` and `ask` rules for guardrails. See [Permissions & safety](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/permissions/).

title: Building from source
summary: Compile Rusty IDE yourself on macOS, Windows or Linux.

sections.text:
Most people should install the [signed DMG](https://rusty-edit.dev/download/). Build from source if you want to hack on Rusty, or to try it on a platform that has no published build.

> [!NOTE]
> Only macOS builds are published and verified. Windows and Linux packaging exists, but those builds are unverified, and the Windows builds are not code-signed.

sections.heading: Prerequisites
sections.text:
All platforms need:

- [Node.js](https://nodejs.org/) 20.19+ or 22.12+
- [Rust](https://www.rust-lang.org/tools/install) (stable toolchain)
- A **sibling checkout** of [`rusty-core`](https://github.com/traian18/rusty-core), the Rust agent engine

`rusty-ide` depends on `rusty-core` by relative path, so Cargo does not fetch it. It has to exist on disk next to the IDE repository:

```text
some-parent-dir/
  rusty-ide/     <- https://github.com/traian18/rusty-ide
  rusty-core/    <- https://github.com/traian18/rusty-core
```

Any `cargo` or `npm run tauri` command fails with an unresolved path dependency error if `rusty-core` is missing.

### Platform requirements

| Platform | Requirement |
|----------|-------------|
| **macOS** | Xcode Command Line Tools: `xcode-select --install` |
| **Windows** | Microsoft C++ Build Tools (MSVC v143 and a Windows 10/11 SDK) |
| **Linux** | System libraries, below |

On Debian or Ubuntu:

```bash
sudo apt install -y libwebkit2gtk-4.1-dev libappindicator3-dev librsvg2-dev patchelf libssl-dev
```

For Fedora, Arch and openSUSE package names, see [BUILD.md](https://github.com/traian18/rusty-ide/blob/main/BUILD.md) in the repository.

sections.heading: Install dependencies
sections.text:
Once, from inside `rusty-ide`:

```bash
npm install
npm install --prefix ../rusty-core/sdk/typescript
```

> [!TIP]
> On npm 10.9.8, adding or updating a dependency with a plain `npm install` can fail with `Cannot read properties of null (reading 'edgesOut')`. Use a newer npm for that command instead: `npx --yes npm@11 install <package>`. `npm ci` is not affected.

sections.heading: Run in development
sections.text:
```bash
npm run tauri dev
```

sections.heading: Build the app
sections.text:
The same command works on every platform:

```bash
npm run tauri build
```

It compiles the TypeScript SDK from the sibling `rusty-core`, typechecks and bundles the frontend with Vite, then compiles the Rust app in release mode and bundles it.

To build one specific bundle:

```bash
# macOS: DMG only
npm run tauri build -- --bundles dmg

# Linux
npm run tauri build -- --bundles deb
npm run tauri build -- --bundles rpm

# Windows
npm run tauri build -- --bundles nsis
npm run tauri build -- --bundles msi
```

### Output

| Platform | Location |
|----------|----------|
| macOS app | `src-tauri/target/release/bundle/macos/Rusty-IDE.app` |
| macOS DMG | `src-tauri/target/release/bundle/dmg/` |
| Windows | `src-tauri/target/release/bundle/nsis/` and `bundle/msi/` |
| Linux | `src-tauri/target/release/bundle/deb/` and `bundle/rpm/` |

An AppImage is not published because the bundled agent runtime trips the AppImage tooling. You can build one yourself with `--bundles appimage`.

sections.heading: Provider runtimes
sections.text: The Codex and GitHub Copilot runtimes are not part of the installers. On first sign-in Rusty downloads only that provider's native package into its app data folder and verifies its checksum first. No system Node.js or npm is needed at runtime.

sections.heading: Signing on macOS
sections.text: The macOS bundle configuration signs with the maintainer's Developer ID identity, and releases are notarized in CI. A local release build on macOS therefore expects signing to be set up: an `APPLE_SIGNING_IDENTITY` and, for notarization, an App Store Connect API key. `RELEASING.md` in the repository describes what CI does. For day-to-day development, `npm run tauri dev` does not need any of this.

sections.heading: Verify your changes
sections.text:
```bash
npm run verify
```

This runs the type checks, the theme usage check, the frontend tests, a production build and the Rust tests.

sections.heading: Notes for Windows and Linux
sections.text:
- **Windows.** The installers are not code-signed, so SmartScreen shows an "unknown publisher" warning on first launch: choose **More info → Run anyway**.
- **Linux.** Install the `.deb` with `sudo apt install ./Rusty-IDE_<version>_amd64.deb` or the `.rpm` with `sudo dnf install ./Rusty-IDE-<version>-1.x86_64.rpm`.
- **WSLg (WSL2).** If the window is black, force the software fallbacks: `WEBKIT_DISABLE_COMPOSITING_MODE=1 WEBKIT_DISABLE_DMABUF_RENDERER=1 rusty-ide`.

title: Built-in workflows
summary: Every workflow and profile that ships with Rusty, what each step does, when to use it, and what it hands over to.

sections.text:
Rusty ships **12 profiles** and **20 workflows**, available in every project without any setup. The built-in ones are read-only: choose **Customize a copy** in the Behaviors tab to change one. For how workflows work in general, see [Workflows](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/workflows/).

On this page a step's profile is described by what it can do:

- **Reads only.** Reads the workspace (some also search the web). Cannot write files or run commands.
- **Runs checks, never edits.** Cannot write files. May run approved, non-destructive commands.
- **Can change files.**

sections.heading: Built-in profiles
sections.text:
Each profile has one responsibility, so a workflow can give each step only what it needs. A step's profile, not the chat's skill, sets its tools.

| Profile | What it does | What it can do |
|---------|--------------|----------------|
| **Research** | Investigates external sources and workspace context to produce sourced options and recommendations. | Reads only. Reads the workspace and searches the web. |
| **Analyze** | Explains how the current code works, where a change belongs, and what it may affect. | Reads only. Workspace only. |
| **Plan** | Turns requirements and code findings into an ordered implementation plan. | Reads only. Reads the workspace and searches the web. |
| **Architect** | Designs components, contracts, data flow and failure handling with explicit trade-offs. | Reads only. Reads the workspace and searches the web. |
| **Debug** | Reproduces failures, tests hypotheses and identifies the root cause. | Runs checks, never edits. May run approved commands to reproduce. |
| **Build** | Implements an approved change and checks the result before reporting. | Can change files. Runs focused checks for its assigned task. |
| **Verify** | Independently checks completed work against the request, plan and actual workspace. | Runs checks, never edits. May run approved checks. |
| **Review** | Finds correctness and maintainability issues and returns prioritized, actionable feedback. | Reads only. Cannot run commands. |
| **Security** | Audits trust boundaries, data handling, dependencies and configuration for exploitable risks. | Reads only. Reads the workspace and searches the web. |
| **Document** | Creates accurate documentation and examples grounded in the current implementation. | Can write files and run the project's checks; cannot run other commands. Its instructions limit writing to documentation files. |
| **Refactor** | Improves internal structure while preserving observable behavior. | Can change files. Runs focused checks for its assigned task. |
| **Optimize** | Improves measurable performance using baseline and after-change evidence. | Can change files. Runs focused checks for its assigned task. |

Profiles use explicit tool allow lists. Reviewers can inspect files but cannot edit or run commands. Profiles supply role boundaries; workflow nodes supply scope. The editing profiles (Build, Refactor, Optimize, Debug and Verify) can also search the web, so a failed download or a missing tool can be looked up and fixed. Each profile's completion gate requires real tool activity before the agent may finish (Plan must have read the code, Build must have run a check after its last edit), and acceptance steps judge Verify's criteria one by one.

sections.heading: Stages
sections.text:
Stages are focused runs that stop at a written result. Run the next stage in the same chat and it [builds on that result](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/workflows/#steer-a-long-job-between-stages). Auto can choose any of them. See [Auto flows](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/auto-flows/).

### Research & analyze

**Research → Analyze.** Reads only.

Use it to understand how some existing functionality works, or to compare options, before deciding anything. Research gathers sourced options, trade-offs and a recommendation. Analyze then ties them to how your code actually works.

You get a research brief with sources, then an analysis with file and symbol references, the flow of data and control, risks, and the likely change surface.

Try: *How does sync work, and what are my options for making retries safer?*

With [flow switching](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/auto-flows/#hand-over-mid-run) on, it can hand over to **Debug & plan a fix** or **Security audit & fix plan**.

### Architect & plan

**Architect → Plan.** Reads only.

Use it to turn findings, or a clear requirement, into a design and then an ordered plan, before any code is written. Architect compares at least two alternatives and recommends the simplest design that fits. Plan turns the design into steps another session can carry out.

You get a design (components, contracts, data flow, failure behavior, alternatives rejected) and a plan of numbered steps, each naming the files and symbols to change and an observable acceptance check.

Try: *Design the retry fix: one policy in the queue worker.*

Hands over to: **Research & analyze**, **Debug & plan a fix**.

### Debug & plan a fix

**Debug → Plan.** Cannot edit files.

Use it when something is broken: an error, a failing test, wrong behavior or a regression. Debug establishes expected versus actual behavior, finds the smallest reliable reproduction and names the root cause. Plan turns the recommended fix into steps. Nothing is edited.

You get a diagnosis (reproduction, evidence, hypotheses tested, root cause, the smallest safe fix, the regression test that should cover it) and a fix plan.

Try: *Saving a file twice sometimes duplicates it. Find out why.*

Hands over to: **Research & analyze**, **Security audit & fix plan**.

### Security audit & fix plan

**Security → Plan.** Reads only.

Use it when you want to know whether code is secure. Security identifies the assets and trust boundaries, then inspects input handling, authentication and authorization, secrets, filesystem, network and command boundaries, dependencies and configuration. Plan orders the fixes by severity.

You get findings ranked by likelihood and impact, each with evidence, an attack scenario and a remediation, then a remediation plan.

Try: *Audit the upload endpoint.*

Hands over to: **Debug & plan a fix**.

### Verify & review changes

**Review → Verify.** Cannot edit files.

Use it to independently check work that is already done, yours or an earlier run's. Review first looks for correctness problems, edge cases, regressions and missing tests. Verify then runs appropriate checks and reports what it verified and what it could not.

You get a verdict and prioritized findings, each with a severity, the exact file and symbol, the impact and a concrete fix.

Try: *Check the changes I just made to the sync queue.*

Hands over to: **Debug & plan a fix**, **Security audit & fix plan**.

### Build & verify

**Plan → you approve → Build → Verify → acceptance → manual checks.** Can change files.

Use it to carry out an approved plan or a clearly scoped request. If the chat already holds a plan or design you agreed to (from Architect & plan, Debug & plan a fix or Security audit & fix plan), Plan adopts it and only updates what the code shows is out of date; otherwise it writes one from the request. You approve the plan, Build implements it, and Verify checks every acceptance criterion against the workspace.

You get Verify's summary: what was built, the outcome for each acceptance criterion, what you still need to check by hand, and follow-ups.

Try: *Go ahead and build it.*

Because it can change files, Auto announces that when it starts it (*· can change files*); it does not ask first. It hands over to **Debug & plan a fix** or **Security audit & fix plan**.

sections.heading: Pipelines
sections.text:
Pipelines run a whole job. Auto never starts one by itself: choose one from the **Mode** menu. All of them can change files, and all of them ask you to approve the plan first.

### The Verify loop

Every editing workflow runs the same loop. Each step is told where it stands in the workflow, what the steps before it handed over, and who reads its result. For the mechanics behind it, see [How workflows work](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/how-workflows-work/#a-run-from-start-to-finish).

**Plan** writes requirements with numbered acceptance criteria, and the tasks that change the code. Work that only someone outside the workspace can do (rotating credentials, deployments, rewriting history) stays out of the tasks and is listed in its summary as follow-ups for you.

**You approve the plan** before anything is built. **Approve** starts building. Write notes and choose **Approve** to have the plan revised with your notes first; building then starts without asking you again. **Request changes** revises the plan and shows it to you again. Build, Verify and the final review all work from the plan as you approved it and also see your notes: where your notes, the plan and your original request disagree, your notes win.

**Build** implements the plan. If a command fails, it reads the output and tries another way (an installed `mvn`, another download URL, a web search for the error) rather than stopping, and a check that really cannot run is reported with the exact command for you to run. In Research, design & build, High-risk change, Security remediation and Refactor safely, the plan's tasks are built one at a time, each by a fresh builder and checked by a reviewer before the next one starts.

**Verify** checks every acceptance criterion against the real workspace, reading the changed code and running the project's checks, and reports each one as pass, fail or manual. The acceptance gate sends any failure back to Build with Verify's evidence as its repair list. Build can be entered up to three times, and a run may make at most 40 step attempts in total. A step that shows no sign of life for 10 minutes is cancelled and retried; waiting for you does not count.

**Manual checks** come last: whatever only a person can check (a device, a real service, a visual result) is listed for you with exact steps. Approve when it works. If it does not, describe what you saw and choose **Request changes**: the work goes back to Build with your description and is verified again. Pipelines with a final review or a security recheck ask for that step's own manual checks separately, and only when it has any.

Steps pass each other plain Markdown. Rusty reads the reply itself: a missing status is inferred, a missing summary falls back to the reply text, requirement and task IDs are numbered for you, and an unclear result counts as unverified, never as a pass. A step does not fail because a heading or an ID is missing.

Successful checks can be reused within the run only when their command, selection and workspace fingerprint match. Missing or changing fingerprints force execution. Use fresh checks when results depend on remote services or other external state. No live-model speedup is implied by this reuse policy.

All built-ins can retrieve the complete earlier conversation and handover through a paged context tool. The run trajectory captures effective native model requests after application instructions have been applied, with credential redaction. Large requests are saved as ordered parts, so the trace does not silently lose the end of the prompt.

### Reading the step lists

Each pipeline below lists its steps in the order they run. **You approve** is the plan approval card, **acceptance** is the check on Verify's criteria that sends failed work back, and **manual checks** is the card that lists what only a person can try, shown only when there is something to try. **Task by task** means the plan's tasks are built one at a time by fresh builders, each checked by a reviewer (see [Task queues](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/how-workflows-work/#task-queues)).

### Plan, build, verify

**Plan → you approve → Build → Verify → acceptance → manual checks.** Can change files.

The everyday choice for a change whose path is clear. Plan investigates read-only and writes requirements, acceptance criteria and tasks; you approve the plan; Build implements it and runs the project's checks; Verify checks every criterion against the workspace and sends failures back to Build.

Try: *Add a "copy path" item to the file tree's context menu.*

Hands over to: **Research & analyze**, **Debug & plan a fix**, **Security audit & fix plan**.

### Analyze, plan & build

**Analyze → Plan → you approve → Build → Verify → acceptance → manual checks.** Can change files.

For a change to existing code that should be understood first. Analyze maps how the code works today: the files and symbols, the data and control flow, the change surface, the tests and the risks. Plan builds on that analysis, using the patterns and test locations it found.

Try: *Make the settings store save in the background instead of on every keystroke.*

Hands over to: **Debug & plan a fix**, **Architect & plan**.

### Research, design & build

**Research → Architect → Plan → you approve → Build, task by task → Verify → acceptance → manual checks.** Can change files.

For a feature that rests on unfamiliar libraries, standards or architectural choices. Research gathers sourced options and a recommendation, Architect designs the solution (interfaces, data shapes, boundaries, and why), and Plan breaks the design into small tasks in the Architect's order of work. Each builder follows the design and says what differs when the code makes part of it impossible.

Try: *Add OAuth device-flow sign-in for the GitHub integration.*

Hands over to: **Debug & plan a fix**, **Security audit & fix plan**.

### Fix a bug

**Debug → Plan → you approve → Build → Verify → acceptance → manual checks.** Can change files.

Fixes a failure end to end. Debug reproduces it and finds the root cause. Plan's first task is the regression test the diagnosis specifies, which fails today; the next fixes the cause. Build writes the test, runs it to see it fail for the diagnosed reason, fixes the code, and runs it again to see it pass. Verify confirms the test exercises the reported failure, that the fix addresses the root cause rather than hiding the symptom, and that the tests around it still pass.

Try: *Saving a file twice sometimes duplicates it. Fix it.*

Hands over to: **Research & analyze**, **Security audit & fix plan**.

### High-risk change

**Analyze → Plan → you approve → Build, task by task → Verify → acceptance → Final review → acceptance → manual checks → final review's manual checks.** Can change files.

For changes where mistakes are expensive: shared code, data formats, public interfaces. Analyze maps the blast radius. Plan keeps every task small and safe on its own, puts tests that pin current behavior before the change that could break it, and makes compatibility and rollback explicit criteria. After Verify, a Final review looks at the change as a whole for risk: callers that may break, data compatibility and migrations, partial failure, concurrency, and whether a rollback is possible. A problem it finds sends the work back to Build, then through Verify and the final review again.

Try: *Change the chat file format to store attachments separately, and keep old chats loading.*

Hands over to: **Debug & plan a fix**, **Security audit & fix plan**.

### Security remediation

**Security audit → Plan → you approve → Build, task by task → Verify → acceptance → Security acceptance → acceptance → manual checks → security acceptance checks.** Can change files.

Audit, fix, then re-audit. The audit ranks confirmed findings by severity (S1, S2, …). Plan makes each one a requirement whose acceptance criterion proves the exploit no longer works, highest severity first. Each fix is built at the trust boundary, not only at one call site, with a test that shows the exploit fails where that is feasible. Security acceptance then takes each original finding by its id, confirms it is fixed, looks for bypasses and partial fixes, and checks the fixes introduced no new risk. Anything that needs action outside the workspace, such as rotating a leaked secret, is a manual check with exact steps.

Try: *Find and fix authorization problems in the API routes.*

Hands over to: **Debug & plan a fix**.

### Refactor safely

**Analyze → Plan → you approve → Refactor, task by task → Verify → acceptance → Final review → acceptance → manual checks → final review's manual checks.** Can change files.

Restructures code without changing what it does. Analyze pins the behavior and interfaces that must stay the same. Plan puts tests that pin uncovered behavior first, and every task keeps the project building and the tests passing. The Refactor profile runs the tests before and after each change, and may change a test only for an interface change the plan names. The Final review compares old and new code paths and checks every caller still gets the same results and errors: a behavior change the plan did not call for sends the work back.

Try: *Split the 1,300-line AgentTab component into smaller components without changing behavior.*

Hands over to: **Debug & plan a fix**, **Security audit & fix plan**.
