### Optimize performance

**Analyze → Plan → you approve → Optimize → Verify → acceptance → manual checks.** Can change files.

Makes something measurably faster or lighter. Analyze finds the candidate bottleneck and how to measure it. Plan makes the measurement part of the plan: a baseline with the exact command, the change, then the same measurement again, with each target stated against the baseline. Optimize measures before and after and reports both numbers from real runs only. Verify checks the numbers come from the same command and conditions, reruns the measurement if it can, and runs the tests: a claimed improvement without a real measurement fails.

Try: *Opening a large folder is slow. Make the file tree load faster.*

Hands over to: **Research & analyze**, **Debug & plan a fix**.

### Write documentation

**Analyze → Plan → you approve → Document → Verify → acceptance → Final review → acceptance → manual checks → final review's manual checks.** Can change files.

Writes or updates documentation from the code itself. Analyze finds the gaps and the source of truth. Plan names each document or section, where it lives and who it is for. Document writes for that audience, checks every name, option and default against the code, and runs the examples where it can. Verify checks the same against the code (wrong or stale documentation fails), and the Final review reads the docs as their audience would.

Try: *Document the configuration options of the MCP integration for users.*

Hands over to: **Research & analyze**.

sections.heading: Spec workflows
sections.text:
Five workflows run the steps of [spec-driven development](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/spec-driven-development/). They work on a change folder under `specs/`, write their results into it, and are started from the **Specs** page in the Documentation tab. They have no `route`, so Auto never picks them, and they never hand over to another workflow.

### Survey the project

**Analyze → Write project file → List capabilities.** Reads only.

Reads the repository (or your description of a new project) and writes `specs/project.md` and `specs/onboarding.md`, a list of the capabilities it found with a purpose and the paths to read for each. Writes no capability spec: you review the list first. See [Onboarding an existing project](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/spec-driven-development/#onboarding-an-existing-project).

### Write a capability spec

**Analyze → Write capability spec.** Reads only.

Writes the spec of one capability from the survey's list: it reads the code at the listed paths and its tests, then writes named requirements with *WHEN … THEN* scenarios, without covering the other capabilities' ground. One run per capability, started from the Project page.

### Specify a change

**Analyze → Clarify → Write spec → Checklist.** Reads only.

Reads the project file, the existing capabilities and the code, then sorts what it learned into decided, assumed and unknown. Clarify settles what the code can answer and ranks the few questions only you can answer, each with a recommended answer. The spec is then written with requirements, ids and criteria in *WHEN … THEN* form, a `Capability:` line for each, the assumptions taken and the open questions, and checked once against its own rules before it is saved. Checklist then tests the spec's quality with questions about the writing (complete, clear, consistent, measurable, edge cases covered), ticks the ones the spec answers and saves them as `checklist.md`. Open items are counted on the Specs page and read by Design & tasks. Run again to revise both.

### Design & tasks for a spec

**Design → Check → Tasks.** Reads only.

Writes `design.md` (with a check against the project's principles). Check then compares spec and design: every criterion needs a part of the design and a test, and gaps and conflicts are rated Blocker, Important or Minor. Tasks writes `tasks.md` with that report in hand: small ordered tasks that each name the requirements and criteria they satisfy.

### Implement a spec

**Build (a step plan, a builder and a review for each unticked task) → Verify → acceptance → manual checks.** Can change files.

Has no Plan step and no plan approval: the plan is the change folder. Builds the tasks that are not ticked, then Verify checks every criterion of the spec. The finished tasks are ticked in `tasks.md`, each gets a document under `tasks/`, and `verification.md` and the change's status are updated. See [Implement](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/spec-driven-development/#4-implement).

sections.heading: Where they live
sections.text: The built-in workflows and profiles are part of the app, not files in your workspace, and appear in the Behaviors tab tagged **Built-in**. Their IDs start with `rusty-ide.builtin.`. A copy you customize is saved in `.rusty/workflows/` and `.rusty/profiles/`. See [Profiles & workflows](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/behaviors/) for the format.

title: Code guidelines
summary: Set a project's code style and rules once; every edit is checked against them, next to code health.

sections.text: **Code guidelines** are a project's own style and rules, kept in the repository. Agents read them before editing a file. Every edit is checked against them, and a run cannot finish while its change breaks an error-level rule.

sections.heading: The folder
sections.text:
```text
.rusty/guidelines/
├── rules.json    the rules the host checks
└── style.md      prose guidance, given to the model
```

Commit the folder with the project. Without it, only code health applies. The folder must be spelled `guidelines`; any other name is not read.

Rusty writes `.rusty/.gitignore` so Git keeps only the shared parts of `.rusty` (guidelines, specs, skills, workflows, profiles, canvas) and leaves chats, runs, goals, metrics and traces on your machine. `.rusty/README.md` lists what each part holds. If your repository's own `.gitignore` has a `/.rusty` line, remove it to share the guidelines.

sections.heading: rules.json
sections.text:
```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "limits": { "max_file_lines": 400, "max_function_lines": 60, "max_complexity": 10, "max_params": 5 },
  "detectors": { "large_method": { "threshold": 50 }, "disabled": ["ownership_risk"] },
  "rules": [
    { "id": "no-unwrap", "kind": "pattern", "lang": "rust",
      "query": "(call_expression function: (field_expression field: (field_identifier) @m (#eq? @m \"unwrap\"))) @violation",
      "exclude": ["**/tests/**"], "message": "Return an error instead of unwrap()" },
    { "id": "no-console", "kind": "pattern", "regex": "console\\.log\\(", "applies": ["src/**/*.ts"], "severity": "warn" },
    { "id": "ui-not-core", "kind": "boundary", "applies": ["src/components/**"], "must_not_import": ["src/harness/core/**"] },
    { "id": "small-ui", "kind": "metric", "applies": ["src/components/**"], "max_file_lines": 250 },
    { "id": "naming", "kind": "prose", "text": "Name functions after what they return or do." }
  ]
}
```

The JSON schema is published as `schema/guidelines-v1.schema.json` in rusty-core. Mistakes in the file are all reported at once, and the rules are not checked until it is fixed.

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `limits` | Size and complexity limits for every source file: lines in the file; lines of code, cyclomatic complexity, nesting depth and parameters per function. Test code is not held to the function limits. |
| `detectors` | [Code health](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/repository-analysis) thresholds for this project, over the defaults. The Code Health page and goals measure with them. |
| `rules[].kind` | `pattern` (a `regex` per line, or a tree-sitter `query` for `lang`; a capture named `violation` marks the lines), `metric` (limits for the files the rule applies to), `boundary` (files that must not import files matching `must_not_import`, from the repository index), `prose` (guidance in words, given to the model and never checked by the host). |
| `applies`, `exclude` | Globs relative to the repository root (`*`, `**`, `?`, `{a,b}`; a glob without `/` matches the file name anywhere). |
| `severity` | `error` (blocks finishing; the default), `warn` (reported), `info` (only shown to the model). |
| `message`, `fix` | What a violation says, and how to fix it. |
| `disabled` | Switches a rule off without deleting it. |

sections.heading: style.md
sections.text:
Plain Markdown. Text before the first glob heading applies to every file. A `##` heading whose whole text is a glob in backticks starts a section for those files:

```markdown
Prefer small modules split by responsibility.

## `src/components/**/*.tsx`
One component per file. Hooks start with `use`.
```

sections.heading: How edits are checked
sections.text:
- **On the first edit to a file** in a run, the edit result ends with what applies to it: its rules (severity, id, message) and the outline of the style guide. Each set is shown once per run, so the agent sees the guidelines without having to ask. For the full text of a rule or style section it calls `code_guidelines` with mode `rules`.
- **The system prompt** of every agent that can edit says the project may have guidelines, that the first edit shows them, and that guideline errors must be fixed before finishing.
- **After every edit**, the `edit_file` / `write_file` result ends with a short notice when the edit introduced a violation. Only the rules the host checks run, and only for what the edit introduced.
- **Before finishing**, the completion gate of the single agent and of the Build, Refactor and Optimize profiles runs the check over the files the run changed. Error-level violations the change introduced send the agent back with the list. After the gate's last continuation it lets the run finish.
- **Only what a change introduced counts.** That means violations on lines changed since the last commit, a function that spans a changed line, and a file-size limit only when the file is new or grew. An untidy repository does not block every edit.
- [Goals](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/goals) can require "no guideline errors" in their scope.

sections.heading: The tool
sections.text:
`code_guidelines` is read-only and every model has it, in every mode and workflow step.

| Call | Answer |
|---|---|
| `{"mode": "rules", "targets": ["path"]}` | The rules, limits and style sections that apply to those files. Without targets: every rule and section. |
| `{"mode": "check", "targets": ["path"], "changed_only": true}` | Violations by line with how to fix them. Without `changed_only`, everything in the files. |

Status `not_configured` means the project has no guidelines; `invalid` lists the mistakes in the rules file.

title: Your first workflow
summary: A hands-on tutorial. Read a built-in workflow on the canvas, customize a copy with its own profile and an approval step, then build a checked change from scratch with a verify loop, manual checks and a subflow.

sections.text:
This tutorial takes about half an hour, in three parts that build on each other. You can stop after any of them.

1. **[Read a workflow](#part-1-read-a-workflow-on-the-canvas)** (5 minutes). Open the built-in **Plan, build, verify** and learn what every card and line on the canvas means.
2. **[Customize a copy](#part-2-customize-a-copy)** (10 minutes). Make **Research with a risk list**: a copy of **Research & analyze** whose second step has its own read-only profile, with an approval step between the two so you can steer it.
3. **[Build one from scratch](#part-3-build-a-checked-change-from-scratch)** (15 minutes). Make **Checked change**: Build, then a Check step that reports every criterion, an acceptance step that sends failures back to Build, and manual checks for you. Then put a subflow in front of it.

You will use four things, each of which has its own page if you want the full detail:

- a **workflow**, the graph of steps ([How workflows work](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/how-workflows-work/));
- a **profile**, what one step may do ([Built-in workflows](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/built-in-workflows/#built-in-profiles));
- the **Behaviors** tab, where both are edited ([The workflow editor](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/workflow-editor/));
- the **Mode** menu in Agent Mode, where you run it ([Workflows](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/workflows/)).

> [!NOTE]
> You need a workspace open and a model connected. If you have not done that, start with the [Quickstart](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/quickstart/).

sections.heading: Part 1: Read a workflow on the canvas
sections.text:
1. Open **Behaviors** in the left rail. The switch at the top left reads **Workflows**.
2. In the list, select **Plan, build, verify**. It carries a **Built-in** badge, and the inspector on the right says *Built into Rusty · available in every project*. Everything is read-only, so click around freely.

The canvas reads left to right: **Request → Plan → Plan approval → Build → Verify → Acceptance → Manual checks → Result**. Each card is a step, with its kind as a badge and its id below its name:

| Badge | What the card shows |
|-------|---------------------|
| **input** | Where the run starts: your message, the chat's last result and your attachments. |
| **agent** | A step that runs a model: its tool setting (*inherit* means everything the chat has, which the profile then narrows), the start of its instructions, and its **profile**. Click the profile name, or double-click the card, to open the profile. |
| **approval** | A point where the run waits for you: which step's result you **review**, where **changes go to**, whether the run may **auto-approve** it, and, for the plan approval, that **approval notes revise first**. |
| **verify** | A check that runs no model: how many **checks** it has, and which step it **retries** when one fails. |
| **output** | Which step's result becomes the run's result. |

The dotted lines below the cards are the loops:

- **changes** from **Plan approval** back to **Plan**: your notes revise the plan.
- **retry** from **Acceptance** back to **Build**: a failed criterion sends the work back.
- **changes** from **Manual checks** back to **Build**: what you report after trying the result.

Now click a few cards and read the inspector:

- **Build.** Its **Instructions** are long on purpose. They tell the step its place (*You are Build, step 3 of 6*), what it is given, what to do, and who checks its result. Under **Context from earlier steps**, the ticked boxes are what Build receives. **Attempts** is 3: Build can be sent back twice.
- **Acceptance.** **Checks** is `[{"type": "criteria", ...}]`: it reads the criteria Verify reported, one by one. **On failure, retry** is **Build**.
- **Manual checks.** **Review the result of** is **Acceptance**, and **Requested changes go to** is **Build**.

That is the whole mechanism: agent steps do work, verify and approval steps decide whether it moves on or goes back. [How workflows work](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/how-workflows-work/) explains each part in depth.

sections.heading: Part 2: Customize a copy
sections.text:
You will make **Research with a risk list**. It investigates a question like the built-in **Research & analyze** stage does, but its second step is read-only by construction, always ends with the riskiest places in the code, and only starts once you have approved the research.

### Why copy instead of starting blank

The 15 built-in workflows are read-only, and they are carefully tuned: every step is told its place in the workflow, they pass written handoffs between steps, and they retry after errors. Starting from a copy keeps all of that and lets you change only what you care about. Everything in the editor works the same on a copy as on a workflow you wrote yourself.

### 1. Make a profile for the second step

A **profile** sets a step's instructions, tools, limits and checks. You will write one that can read the code but never change it.

1. Open **Behaviors** in the left rail.
2. Click **Profiles** in the switch at the top left.
3. Click **New profile**, type the id `risk-analyst` and press <kbd>Enter</kbd>. Ids use lowercase letters, digits, dots, dashes and underscores. The editor saves it as `.rusty/profiles/risk-analyst.json` and selects it.
4. In the inspector on the right, under **Profile**, set **Status** to **Published**. A new profile starts as a draft.
5. Under **Instructions**, leave **Mode** on *Append to the system prompt* and write in **Text**:

   ```text
   Trace how the code behind the question works. Finish with a section called
   "Riskiest places": the three files or functions most likely to break if
   this area changes, each with the file path and one sentence on why.
   ```

6. Under **Tools**, set **Available tools** to **Only these tools** and tick **Read Files**, **List Files**, **Search Codebase**, **Project Info** and **Read Workflow Context**. Leave everything that writes or runs commands unticked, so the step cannot change anything. (Searching for a tool by name is quicker than scrolling: use the **Search tools** box.)
7. Under **Model and limits**, set **Max turns** to `40` so the step cannot loop forever.

Leave **Rules** and **Completion gate** empty for now. They are covered in [Going further](#going-further).

> [!TIP]
> The checkboxes decide what the step is *offered*. The session's own permissions still apply on top, so a step can only ever use tools that both the profile allows and the session enables. See [Permissions & safety](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/permissions/).

### 2. Copy a built-in workflow

1. Click **Workflows** in the switch at the top left.
2. In the list, select **Research & analyze**. It carries a **Built-in** badge, and the inspector says *Built into Rusty · available in every project*.
3. Click **New workflow**, or **Customize a copy** at the top of the inspector. Both open the same dialog.
4. Type the id `risk-research` and click **Create**.

You now have an independent, editable copy, saved as `.rusty/workflows/risk-research.json` once you save. It starts as a copy of whichever built-in workflow was selected, with its revision reset to 1 and its name set to the id.

> [!NOTE]
> **New workflow** copies the built-in that is selected. With one of *your own* workflows selected instead, it starts from a small blank flow. [Part 3](#part-3-build-a-checked-change-from-scratch) uses that.

### 3. Make it yours

The canvas shows the copy: **Request → Research → Analyze → Result**.

**Name it.** Click an empty part of the canvas so nothing is selected. The inspector shows the workflow itself. Set **Name** to `Research with a risk list` and **Description** to one sentence, such as *Investigate a question, then list the riskiest places in the code.* The description is what you read when you hover the workflow in the Mode menu. Bump **Revision** whenever you change a workflow you have already used, so you can tell versions apart.

**Give Analyze the profile.**

1. Click the **Analyze** step.
2. Under **Behavior**, open the **Profile** menu and choose `risk-analyst`.

The step keeps its instructions and its inputs; only what it is allowed to do changes. It can no longer write files or run commands, whatever its instructions say.

**Look at what the step receives.** Still on **Analyze**, scroll to the **Step** section. Under **Context from earlier steps**, **Original request** and **Research** are ticked: Analyze receives your request (and the chat's last result) plus Research's final message. **Response format** is **Text / Markdown**, so Research's message arrives as written. Leave **Tools** on **Everything the session has**: the profile already narrows them.

### 4. Add an approval step

Research runs first and Analyze builds on it. If Research goes the wrong way, Analyze goes with it. An approval step between them lets you read the research and correct it before Analyze starts.

1. Click **Approval** above the canvas. A step named **Approval** (id `approval`) appears. Drag it between **Research** and **Analyze**.
2. Click the arrow from **Research** to **Analyze** and choose **Delete edge**. Deleting it also takes Research's result away from Analyze; you will give it back in step 5.
3. Drag from **Research**'s right handle to **Approval**, then from **Approval**'s right handle to **Analyze**. Connecting Approval to Analyze also hands Analyze the approval's result: your decision and any notes you wrote.
4. Select **Approval** and set:
   - **Name**: `Approve the research`.
   - **Review the result of**: **Research**.
   - **Question**: `Read the research. Approve it to go on to Analyze, or ask for changes.`
   - Leave **Requested changes go to** on **The step being reviewed**, so changes go back to Research.
5. Select **Analyze** and, under **Context from earlier steps**, tick **Research** again.

A dotted **changes** line now runs from **Approve the research** back to **Research**.

### 5. Save and check

The button at the top right reads **Save 2**: two files changed, the profile and the workflow. Press <kbd>⌘</kbd> <kbd>S</kbd> or click it. The button goes back to **Saved**.

The editor validates everything as you type. A red dot beside a file in the list means it has a problem, and the inspector lists it. A file with a blocking problem still saves, but an invalid profile is skipped when sessions load, so fix a red dot before you rely on the file.

### 6. Run it

1. Click **Run in Agent Mode**. It saves anything unsaved, selects the workflow in Agent Mode and opens the chat. If the workflow has a blocking problem, it tells you instead of running.
2. In the workflow bar, the **Mode** menu now reads **Stage: Research with a risk list**. It is labelled *Stage* because the copy kept the built-in's metadata. Workflows you make from scratch are labelled **Workflow:**.
3. Ask a real question about your project, such as *How does the settings store save its data?*, and press <kbd>Enter</kbd>.

The bar lists the steps and where the run is, for example *Running step 2 of 5: Research*. When Research finishes, the bar shows the approval step *waiting for your answer*, and a card opens above the message box: **Approve the research needs your answer**, with your question and Research's findings.

Try both ways through it:

- Write a correction in **Notes**, such as *Also look at how the store migrates old settings*, and choose **Request changes**. Research runs again with your notes and its previous findings, and the card comes back with the revised research.
- Choose **Approve**. Analyze starts, with the research and your approval.

When it finishes, read the last message: Analyze's handoff, ending with **Riskiest places**. Because no step can change files, Rusty also saves it as a Markdown file under `.rusty/findings/` and says where.

Back in the Behaviors tab, the canvas carries a badge such as *Last run completed*, and each step shows its own state.

If something went wrong, the bar says which step failed and your next message resumes there. Steps that finished are kept. See [Run a workflow](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/workflows/#run-a-workflow).

sections.heading: Part 3: Build a checked change from scratch
sections.text:
You will make **Checked change**: a workflow that builds a change, has an independent step check every requirement, sends failures back to the builder automatically, and gives you the checks only a person can do. It is a small version of the built-in pipelines, and by the end it uses every kind of step.

```text
Input → Build → Check → Acceptance → Manual checks → Output
          ↑                  │             │
          ├─ retry ──────────┘             │
          └─ changes ──────────────────────┘
```

### 1. Start from the blank flow

1. In the list, select **Research with a risk list** (one of your own) and click **New workflow**.
2. Type the id `checked-change` and click **Create**.

With one of your own workflows selected, **New workflow** starts from a small blank flow: **Input → Execute → Verify → Output**. Execute and Verify are both *agent* steps here, with short placeholder instructions. Click the empty canvas and set **Name** to `Checked change`.

### 2. The Build step

Select **Execute** (id `execute`) and set:

- **Name**: `Build`.
- **Profile**: `rusty-ide.builtin.build`. Built-in profiles are listed under their full ids. Build can change files, must run the project's checks after its last edit, and reports what it did.
- **Instructions**:

  ```text
  Implement the request in the workspace. Read the code before changing it,
  add or update tests, and run the project's checks. Finish with a report:
  what you changed and where, the checks you ran and their results, and
  anything left for me.
  ```

- **Attempts**: `3`, so the work can come back to Build twice.

Under **Context from earlier steps**, **Input** is already ticked: Build receives your request.

### 3. The Check step

Select **Verify** (id `verify`; it is an agent step, despite the name) and set:

- **Name**: `Check`.
- **Profile**: `rusty-ide.builtin.verify`. It can read files and run checks, but never edit.
- Under **Context from earlier steps**, tick **Input** as well, so Check sees the request and not only Build's report. Do this before the next setting: the checkboxes are only shown for Text / Markdown steps.
- **Instructions**:

  ```text
  Check the change against the request in the real workspace. Read the
  changed code and run the project's checks. Report every requirement of
  the request, and every problem you find, as a criterion: pass when it is
  done properly, fail followed by what is wrong and where, manual only for
  what needs a person (then give the exact steps in how_to_test). Do not
  edit files.
  ```

- **Response format**: **JSON with host validation**. The acceptance step needs Check's criteria as data it can read one by one.

Then open **Advanced data mapping** and replace **Output schema** with the shape of a report. This is the same shape the built-in Verify steps use:

```json
{
  "type": "inline", "name": "check",
  "schema": {
    "type": "object", "additionalProperties": false, "required": ["criteria", "summary"],
    "properties": {
      "criteria": {
        "type": "array",
        "items": {
          "type": "object", "additionalProperties": false,
          "required": ["id", "status", "evidence", "how_to_test"],
          "properties": {
            "id": { "type": "string", "minLength": 1 },
            "status": { "type": "string", "enum": ["pass", "fail", "manual"] },
            "evidence": { "type": "string", "minLength": 1 },
            "how_to_test": { "type": "string" }
          }
        }
      },
      "summary": { "type": "string", "minLength": 1 }
    }
  }
}
```

The model does not have to write JSON: it is asked for a Markdown section per field, and Rusty reads its reply into this shape.

### 4. The Acceptance step

1. Click **Verify** above the canvas. This adds a real verify step, which runs no model. Its id is `verify_2`, because `verify` is taken.
2. Set **Name** to `Acceptance`.
3. Replace **Checks** with:

   ```json
   [{ "type": "criteria", "pointer": "/check/criteria" }]
   ```

4. Set **On failure, retry** to **Build**.
5. Open **Advanced data mapping** and set **Input bindings** to:

   ```json
   [{ "target": "check", "source": { "type": "node_output", "node_id": "verify", "pointer": "" } }]
   ```

   This hands Check's report to Acceptance under the name `check`, which is why the check's pointer starts with `/check`.
6. Rewire: delete the edge from **Check** to **Output**, then connect **Check** to **Acceptance**.

The editor now lists a few problems. Two go away in step 5, once Acceptance leads somewhere and Output can be reached again. One needs fixing now: *retry target execute must list verification_failed in retry_on*. A step may only be sent back for a failed check when its own retry settings accept that reason. Click **Edit as JSON** at the top of the inspector, find the step with `"id": "execute"`, and change its `retry` to:

```json
"retry": { "max_attempts": 3, "retry_on": ["verification_failed"] }
```

Click **Show form** to go back. That problem is gone, and a dotted **retry** line runs from Acceptance back to Build.

### 5. The Manual checks step

1. Click **Approval** above the canvas (id `approval`).
2. Connect **Acceptance** to it, and it to **Output**.
3. Select it and set:
   - **Name**: `Manual checks`.
   - **Review the result of**: **Acceptance**.
   - **Question**: `Verification passed. Try the manual checks listed below, then Approve, or describe what does not work and choose Request changes.`
   - **Requested changes go to**: **Build**.
   - **Skip when empty at**: `/manual_checks`. Acceptance collects the criteria Check marked **manual** there; when there are none, you are not asked at all.

### 6. The Output step

Select **Output**. **Show the final message from** is already **Check**, so the result is every criterion with its status and evidence, then the summary. To show only the summary, open **Advanced source mapping** and change `"pointer": ""` to `"pointer": "/summary"`.

### 7. Save and run

Press <kbd>⌘</kbd> <kbd>S</kbd>. If a step still shows a red mark, hover it or select the step to read the problem. Then click **Run in Agent Mode**; the Mode menu reads **Workflow: Checked change**. Ask for a small, real change, such as *Add a `--version` flag to the CLI*.

What you will see:

1. **Build** changes the code and runs the checks. Rusty asks before each command; allow the ones you recognize.
2. **Check** reads the change, runs the checks, and reports each requirement as pass, fail or manual.
3. **Acceptance** passes when nothing failed. If something did, the chat says *Acceptance sent the work back; running Build again (attempt 2)*, and Build receives each failed criterion with its evidence as its repair list. After three Build attempts the run fails at Acceptance.
4. **Manual checks** opens a card only when Check left something for a person. **Request changes** sends your description back to Build, and the whole loop runs again.
5. The result is Check's report.

If you get lost, click **Edit as JSON** and compare with the complete file:

```json
{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "id": "checked-change",
  "revision": 1,
  "name": "Checked change",
  "status": "draft",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "input", "name": "Input", "type": "input", "config": { "defaults": {} } },
    {
      "id": "execute", "name": "Build", "type": "agent",
      "config": {
        "instructions": "Implement the request in the workspace. ...",
        "profile": { "id": "rusty-ide.builtin.build" },
        "tools": { "type": "inherit" },
        "context_mode": "isolated_child",
        "structured_output": "text"
      },
      "input_bindings": [
        { "target": "request", "source": { "type": "node_output", "node_id": "input", "pointer": "/request" } }
      ],
      "output_schema": { "type": "inline", "name": "written_handoff", "schema": { "type": "string" } },
      "retry": { "max_attempts": 3, "retry_on": ["verification_failed"] }
    },
    {
      "id": "verify", "name": "Check", "type": "agent",
      "config": {
        "instructions": "Check the change against the request in the real workspace. ...",
        "profile": { "id": "rusty-ide.builtin.verify" },
        "tools": { "type": "inherit" },
        "context_mode": "isolated_child",
        "structured_output": "host_validated"
      },
      "input_bindings": [
        { "target": "report", "source": { "type": "node_output", "node_id": "execute", "pointer": "" } },
        { "target": "input", "source": { "type": "node_output", "node_id": "input", "pointer": "" } }
      ],
      "output_schema": { "type": "inline", "name": "check", "schema": { "...": "the schema from step 3" } }
    },
    {
      "id": "verify_2", "name": "Acceptance", "type": "verify",
      "config": { "checks": [{ "type": "criteria", "pointer": "/check/criteria" }], "retry_target": "execute" },
      "input_bindings": [
        { "target": "check", "source": { "type": "node_output", "node_id": "verify", "pointer": "" } }
      ]
    },
    {
      "id": "approval", "name": "Manual checks", "type": "approval",
      "config": {
        "subject": { "type": "node_output", "node_id": "verify_2", "pointer": "" },
        "prompt": "Verification passed. Try the manual checks listed below, ...",
        "revise_target": "execute",
        "skip_if_empty": "/manual_checks",
        "max_revisions": 5,
        "allow_auto_approve": true
      }
    },
    {
      "id": "output", "name": "Output", "type": "output",
      "config": { "source": { "type": "node_output", "node_id": "verify", "pointer": "" }, "strict": false }
    }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "id": "input-execute", "source": "input", "target": "execute", "condition": "on_success" },
    { "id": "execute-verify", "source": "execute", "target": "verify", "condition": "on_success" },
    { "id": "verify_to_verify_2", "source": "verify", "target": "verify_2", "condition": "on_success" },
    { "id": "verify_2_to_approval", "source": "verify_2", "target": "approval", "condition": "on_success" },
    { "id": "approval_to_output", "source": "approval", "target": "output", "condition": "on_success" }
  ]
}
```

The `...` parts are shortened here; your file has the full texts and schema. The editor also stores each card's position under `metadata.editor.position`, which the engine ignores.

### 8. Investigate first, with a subflow

A subflow runs a whole workflow as one step. Put the built-in **Research & analyze** in front of Build, so Build starts from an investigation instead of from nothing.

1. Click **Subflow** above the canvas (id `subflow`) and set **Name** to `Investigate`.
2. Set **Run** to **A saved workflow** and **Workflow** to `rusty-ide.builtin.investigate`. Every built-in workflow is listed under its full id, next to your own.
3. Open **Advanced data mapping** and set **Input bindings** to:

   ```json
   [
     { "target": "request", "source": { "type": "run_input", "pointer": "/request" } },
     { "target": "context", "source": { "type": "run_input", "pointer": "/context" } }
   ]
   ```

   What is bound to a subflow step is the child run's whole input, and the built-in workflows read both `request` and `context`.
4. Rewire: delete the edge from **Input** to **Build**, then connect **Input** to **Investigate** and **Investigate** to **Build**. Connecting it to Build hands Build the investigation.

Save and run it again. Investigate runs Research & analyze as one step, then Build starts with its findings. Permission prompts and approvals from inside the subflow appear in your chat as usual.

sections.heading: Going further
sections.text:
### Add a rule

Rules react to events during a step. Open `risk-analyst` in the **Profiles** view and, under **Rules**, pick an event and an action beside **Add rule**, then click it. For example, to remind the agent of something when the step starts:

| Event | Action | Then set |
|-------|--------|----------|
| `RunStart` | `inject` | **Inject text**: *Cite the file path for every claim you make.* |

The text is added to the model's context when the rule fires. The same mechanism can refuse a tool call (`deny`), ask you first (`ask`), or stop the run (`stop_run`). The full list of events, actions and conditions is in [The workflow editor](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/workflow-editor/#rules).

### Add a completion check

A completion gate stops an agent from finishing too early. Under **Completion gate**, click **Add completion check**. The new check uses the method **Check tool activity** and, by default, requires at least one **Run Commands** call. That is wrong for a read-only step, so change it: under the check's condition (*Tool call count*), untick **Run Commands** and tick **Read Files** and **Search Codebase**, with **At least** set to `1`. Then write the **Feedback when this check fails**, which is what the agent receives when it tries to finish without looking at the code: *Read the relevant files before answering.* **If checks still fail** decides what happens after the allowed **Additional attempts**: **Fail the run** is strict, **Finish with checks not passed** lets the step through anyway.

### Make Rusty choose it

A workflow written with a `route.when` sentence in its `metadata` is a candidate for [Auto](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/auto-flows/): Rusty reads the sentence and picks it when a request fits. The copy you made inherited one from *Research & analyze*, so Auto may already pick your copy for the same kind of question. To change that, open the JSON view (the file icon at the top of the inspector, **Edit as JSON**) and edit `metadata.route.when` or delete `metadata.route`. See [Choosing and switching flows](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/behaviors/#choosing-and-switching-flows).

### Let an agent write it

You can also describe a workflow in words and let an agent build it. In a **Single agent** chat, choose the **workflow-author** skill and describe what you want, for example *a workflow that fixes lint errors one file at a time and asks me before touching tests*. It reads your existing workflows and profiles, asks only about what is still unclear, and saves a complete, validated workflow. It does not run it: select it in the Mode menu and run it yourself. See [Workflow Author skill](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/skills/#workflow-author-skill-create-a-workflow-by-describing-it).

title: Goals
summary: Tell the agent what to do and what counts as done; it works in passes until the measurement says the goal is reached.

sections.text:
A **goal** is an instruction plus a result that counts as done. The agent works on it in **passes**. Each pass is a fresh single-agent run in the same chat. After each pass, Rusty measures the code and decides whether to go on. The agent never ends a goal by saying it is finished: the measurement decides.

A goal can be any kind of work:

- a **task goal**, any instruction ("add CSV export to the report page", "migrate the settings to the new store", "document every public module"): the first pass plans it, later passes carry the plan on, and it ends when the plan is finished, the checks pass and the result is judged done;
- a **quality goal**, with a code health target (`health=`, `mean=` or `severity=`): it ends when the measurement says so, for work like "rewrite this module until it is healthy".

sections.heading: Starting a goal
sections.text:
Type `/goal` in the Agent tab, followed by options and what to do. There is no other format to learn: the options are optional `key=value` pairs at the start, and everything after them is the instruction, in your own words. Say what you want and what counts as done; the first pass works out the plan from it.

```text
/goal Add CSV export to the report page; the export button downloads every visible column
/goal checks=typecheck,test scope="the task queue and whatever schedules it" Make retries back off exponentially
/goal mean=8.5 health=6 Raise rusty-core's code health; split the worst files by responsibility
/goal scope=src/harness/core/run/** health=8.5 checks=typecheck,test Split CoreRun into smaller modules
```

Quote a value that has spaces. Unquoted words that are not paths (`scope=The health is ...`) are read as the start of the instruction.

| Option | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `scope="in words"` | The scope as a description (quoted, with spaces). The passes work out the files from it and keep their plan within it. A code health goal is measured on the repository it or the instruction names. |
| `scope=a,b` | Paths: files, folders or globs the targets are measured on (`scope=rusty-core`, `scope=src/**/*.rs`); `scope=changed` means the files the passes change. Attached files are added. A scope that names no file, folder or glob is refused. Without a scope, a goal on code health is measured on the repository the instruction names, else the active one; a goal with only checks measures the files the passes change. |
| `health=8.5` | Every file in scope has a [code health](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/repository-analysis) score of at least this (1-10). Only structure counts; change history is not something a pass can fix. |
| `mean=8.5` | The mean score of the files in scope is at least this. Like `health=`, it counts structure only, so it can be higher than the Code Health page's score, which includes change history. |
| `severity=medium` | No code health finding in scope is more severe than `low`, `medium`, `high` or `critical`. |
| `checks=typecheck,test` | Checks that must pass. Each pass runs them with `run_check`; only a whole check run after the pass's last edit counts. |
| `loops=8` | Passes before the goal pauses (`passes=` is the same, 1 to 100). Without it there is no limit: passes go on until the goal is done, blocked, or three passes in a row make no progress. |
| `guidelines=off` | Do not require "no [guideline](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/code-guidelines) errors" (on by default). |
| `keep=all` | Keep a pass even when it makes things worse (by default it is undone). |
| `done="..."` | A result in words. The [reviewer](#the-reviewer) judges it, and its answer counts only once every measured target is met. |

With no code health target, the goal is a task goal. A goal needs a skill selected, because its passes run on the single agent.

sections.heading: Task goals
sections.text:
```text
/goal checks=typecheck,test Add CSV export to the report page
```

1. **The first pass plans the whole goal**: it reads what it needs, then writes every step to the result as its to-do list, each naming the files or area, the change and how it is verified.
2. **The plan is kept** in the goal file. Each later pass is shown the plan as it stands (`[x]` done, `[ ]` open), re-posts it, adds steps it has found, and takes the next open steps. A step is marked done only once it is verified.
3. **Done** needs all of: every step closed (completed, or cancelled because it turned out unnecessary), every check the pass ran passing (plus the `checks=` you asked for), no guideline errors in the changed files, and the [reviewer](#the-reviewer) judging the goal done. The agent saying it is done is not enough. A pass that cancels more steps than it completes has them reopened.
4. **Progress** is more steps done, fewer failing checks, or code changed while the plan is worked (a large step can take more than one pass). New code may score lower than old code, so a task pass is undone only when it breaks a check that passed or adds guideline errors.

To add a quality bar to a task, measure only what it changes: `/goal health=8 scope=changed Add CSV export`.

sections.heading: Each pass of a quality goal
The reviewer
sections.text:
After every pass, before Rusty decides, a reviewer reads what the pass left: its diff since the checkpoint, the checks, the plan and the agent's final message. It is one call to the chat's model with no tools, and it answers **done**, **continue** (with what is missing and the next concrete step) or **blocked**. The agent's own claims are not evidence to it: a pass cannot end its goal by saying it is done, or that the work is too large or risky to start.

- **Blocked** is only for what you alone can provide: a decision, a credential, a value that is in neither the code nor its history, or a manual step. Large, risky or coordinated work is never a blocker.
- The reviewer's next step is the first thing the next pass is told to take on.
- If the reviewer gives no usable answer, the pass's own `Status:` and `Done when:` lines are used instead.

sections.heading: Controlling a goal
sections.text:
| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `/goal` or `/goal status` | Shows the chat's goal: status, passes used, where it stands. |
| `/goal pause` | Stops after the running pass. |
| `/goal resume` | Measures again and starts the `loops=` count afresh. |
| `/goal clear` | Deletes the goal. |

Sending any other message pauses a running goal: you have taken over. A pass that fails or is stopped also pauses it.

sections.heading: Where goals are kept
sections.text: Each goal is a file in the workspace, `.rusty/goals/<id>.json`, which holds its targets, the measurement it started from, the last accepted measurement and a journal of the passes. Next to it, `<id>.checkpoint.json` names the snapshot the running pass started from.

title: How workflows work
summary: The parts of a workflow, what happens at each step of a run, how work is handed on, sent back and approved, and the limits that keep every run bounded.

sections.text: [Workflows](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/workflows/) shows how to run one. This page explains what happens underneath, so you can predict what a run will do, read any workflow on the canvas, and build your own.

sections.heading: The model in one minute
sections.text:
A workflow is a small graph saved as one JSON file:

- **Steps** do the work. Most are **agent steps**: each one starts a fresh agent with its own instructions and tools, and ends with a written result.
- **Edges** say which step comes next.
- **Bindings** say what each step is given: your request, what came before, and the results of earlier steps.
- **Verify steps** and **approval steps** can send work back to an earlier step, with the reason, instead of letting it through.
- **Limits** cap attempts, steps, tokens, cost and time, so a run cannot loop forever.

The Behaviors tab draws the file as a canvas, and Rusty's workflow engine checks it before every run. A workflow the engine cannot run safely, for example one with a cycle, is refused before anything starts, and the editor shows why.

sections.heading: A run from start to finish
sections.text:
This is the everyday **Plan, build, verify** workflow after its **Request** step, the way the canvas lays it out. The arrows on the first line are edges. The lines below are the two ways work goes back: a failed check (**retry**) and a person asking for something else (**changes**).

```text
Plan → Plan approval → Build → Verify → Acceptance → Manual checks → Result
  ↑          │           ↑                   │             │
  └ changes ─┘           ├ retry ────────────┘             │
                         └ changes ────────────────────────┘
```

Here is what happens after you press <kbd>Enter</kbd>:

1. **Request** (an input step). The run starts with your message as `request`, the last result in the chat as `context`, and your attached files as `attachments`.
2. **Plan** (an agent step, Plan profile, read-only). A fresh agent reads the request, the context and the code. It writes requirements with numbered acceptance criteria (R1.1, R1.2, …) and the tasks that will change the code. Only its final message moves on; the next steps never see its exploration.
3. **Plan approval** (an approval step). The run pauses and the plan appears in a card above the message box. You approve it, approve it with notes, ask for changes, or reject it. Notes and requested changes go back to Plan, which revises the plan.
4. **Build** (an agent step, Build profile, can change files). Implements the plan you approved, runs the project's checks and reports what it changed.
5. **Verify** (an agent step, Verify profile, cannot edit). Checks every acceptance criterion against the workspace itself, reading the code and running the checks, and reports each criterion as **pass**, **fail** or **manual** with its evidence.
6. **Acceptance** (a verify step; no model runs here). Reads Verify's criteria. Any **fail** sends the work back to Build, with Verify's evidence as the repair list, and Build, Verify and Acceptance run again. **Manual** criteria move on.
7. **Manual checks** (an approval step). When Verify left checks that only a person can do, you get them with exact steps. Approve when they work. Otherwise describe what you saw and choose **Request changes**: the work goes back to Build and is verified again. When there is nothing to check, this step passes without asking.
8. **Result** (an output step). Verify's summary becomes the run's final message in the chat.

Every built-in workflow that changes files follows this pattern. Some add steps before Plan (Analyze, Research, Debug, a security audit), build the plan one task at a time, or add a final review. See [Built-in workflows](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/built-in-workflows/).

sections.heading: The six kinds of step
sections.text:
The buttons above the canvas add one of each.

| Step | Runs a model? | What it does |
|------|---------------|--------------|
| **Input** | No | Starts the run with the run input. A workflow has exactly one. |
| **Agent** | Yes | Runs a fresh agent under a profile and passes on its final message. |
| **Verify** | No | Checks an earlier step's result. When a check fails, it sends the work back, follows a failure edge, or fails the run. |
| **Approval** | No | Pauses the run until you approve, ask for changes, or reject. |
| **Subflow** | Through the flow it runs | Runs another workflow, or a single extra step, inside this one. |
| **Output** | No | Picks the step whose result is the workflow's result. A workflow needs at least one, and nothing may follow it. |

### Input

The input step receives the **run input**. When you send a message in Agent Mode, Rusty sends:

| Field | What it holds |
|-------|---------------|
| `request` | Your message. |
| `context` | The last result in the chat, when a step of the workflow reads it (up to about 24,000 characters). Empty in a new chat. |
| `attachments` | Files you attached. |

**Input defaults** fill in fields the run input does not carry. They apply to steps that read the input step's own result. A step that reads the run input directly (a `run_input` binding, which is what **Original request** adds) sees only what Rusty sent.

### Agent

An agent step is where the work happens. Each one:

- **starts fresh**, in an isolated session that inherits your workspace, the chat's model and your permission settings. It does not see the chat or the other steps' conversations, only what is bound to it;
- **runs under a profile** that sets its role instructions, tools, rules, turn limits and completion checks. With no profile (**Session default**) it runs under the profile the chat already uses;
- **gets the step's own instructions**, followed by its inputs as Markdown in a `workflow_input` block. The prompt tells the agent the inputs are data, not instructions;
- **can use a tool only when three things allow it**: the step's **Tools** setting, the profile's tool list, and the chat's permissions. A command still asks you before it runs;
- **ends with a final message**, which is its result.

The **Response format** decides what that result is. **Text / Markdown** passes the final message on as written; this is the default and what most steps use. The JSON formats return a checked object instead, which a verify step can test field by field. The built-in Verify steps use one so the acceptance check can read each criterion. Models never have to write JSON by hand: the step is asked for Markdown headings that match the fields, and Rusty reads the reply into the object. A missing heading or ID is filled in or inferred, and an unclear result counts as unverified, never as a pass.

An agent step can also run a plan as a [task queue](#task-queues).

### Verify

A verify step runs no model. It reads what is bound to it and applies its **checks**:

| Check | Passes when |
|-------|-------------|
| `criteria` | A list of `{id, status, evidence}` has no failed criterion. `fail` sends the work back. `manual` (only a person can check it) moves on and is collected in the step's `manual_checks`, for an approval step to show you. With `plan_pointer`, every acceptance criterion in the plan must be reported, and one nobody reported counts as missing. |
| `required_status` | The value at a pointer equals a given text, for example `/status` equals `done`. |
| `artifact_exists` | The value at a pointer is present and not empty. |
| `artifacts_resolvable` | Every `{kind, reference}` entry in a list really resolves in the workspace, for example a file that exists, rather than trusting the model's claim. |
| `schema` | Every bound result matches the output schema of the step that produced it. |
| `requirements_satisfied` | Every expected acceptance criterion has exactly one passing, evidenced result. |

When every check passes, the run moves on. When one fails, the step sends the work back to its **retry target** ([below](#sending-work-back)). Without one, the run follows the step's failure edge if it has one, and otherwise fails at this step.

### Approval

An approval step pauses the run and puts a card above the message box: the step's question, the result you are reviewing, a notes box and three buttons.

| Button | What happens |
|--------|--------------|
| **Approve** | The run continues. Notes you wrote are part of the approval's result, so later steps bound to it can read them. |
| **Request changes** | Needs notes. The work goes back to the **revise target** (by default, the step whose result you are reviewing) with your notes as the changes to make. That step sees its previous result and your words, revises it, and every step in between runs again. Then you are asked again. |
| **Reject** | The run ends, with your notes as the reason. |

Settings that change this behavior:

- **Notes given with an approval revise the result first.** Approving with notes then works like requesting changes, except that once the result is revised, the approval stands and you are not asked again. The built-in plan approvals work this way.
- **Times changes may be asked for** (5 by default, at most 10). After that, the card offers only Approve and Reject. Asking for changes does not use up the target step's attempts.
- **Skip when empty at.** A pointer into what is reviewed. When nothing is there, the step passes without asking. The built-in **Manual checks** steps use this, so you are only asked when there is something to try.
- **Auto mode.** A checkbox in the workflow bar approves every step, including those marked **Always ask a person, even when the run auto-approves**, and answers every other prompt. See [Auto mode](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/agent-mode/#auto-mode).

### Subflow

A subflow step runs another workflow, or one extra agent step, in the middle of this one: to research something first, to fix a bug found on the way, and so on.

- **Run a saved workflow**: any workflow in your workspace, or a built-in one by its full id, such as `rusty-ide.builtin.investigate` for Research & analyze.
- **Run a single step**: an agent with the instructions and profile you give it.

What is bound to the subflow step becomes the child run's input, and the child's result becomes this step's result. The child uses the same model, tools and permissions, and its permission prompts and approvals appear in your chat like any other. Flows can call flows up to three levels deep.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Bind every field the child reads. The built-in workflows read `request` and `context`, so a subflow that runs one needs both bindings, usually straight from the run input. Input defaults do not fill them in.

### Output

The output step names the step whose result is the run's result: **Show the final message from** a step. A pointer can pick one field of a structured result; the built-in pipelines show Verify's `/summary`. The output step must come last.

sections.heading: How work is handed on
sections.text:
A step sees only what is **bound** to it. Each binding has a name, which is what the agent sees in its `workflow_input`, and a source:

| Source | Reads | Example |
|--------|-------|---------|
| `run_input` | A field of the run input. | `{"type": "run_input", "pointer": "/request"}` |
| `node_output` | The result of an earlier step, or one field of it. | `{"type": "node_output", "node_id": "plan", "pointer": ""}` |

A pointer of `""` means the whole result; `/summary` means its `summary` field. A step can read only steps that are certain to have run before it.

You rarely write bindings by hand. In the editor, connecting one step to a **Text / Markdown** agent step binds the first step's result to the second, and the **Context from earlier steps** checkboxes add or remove bindings. Use **Advanced data mapping** for anything else.

Two things are easy to miss:

- **Only the final message moves on.** The next step does not see a step's tool calls or reasoning, so a step's final message has to say everything the next one needs. The built-in steps are told so.
- **A workflow that does not read `context`** still hears about the conversation. Rusty puts your earlier requests and the last result behind the new request, marked as background, so a follow-up such as "now fix what you found" does not start from nothing.

sections.heading: The order of steps
Sending work back
sections.text:
There are two ways, and both re-run every step between the target and the step that sent the work back.

| | Verify step | Approval step |
|---|---|---|
| **Triggered by** | A failed check. | You choose **Request changes**, or approve with notes when the step revises on notes. |
| **Goes back to** | Its retry target: **On failure, retry**. | Its revise target: **Requested changes go to**. By default, the step whose result you reviewed. |
| **The target is told** | Why the attempt was rejected. For a `criteria` check, each failed criterion with its evidence. | Your notes, word for word, as the changes to make, together with its previous result. |
| **How many times** | Until the target runs out of **Attempts**. | Up to **Times changes may be asked for**. It does not use up the target's attempts. |
| **Target requirements** | An agent step that runs before the verify step, whose retry list includes `verification_failed`. | An agent step that runs before the approval step. |

Failure reasons reach the target as data: it is told to address them, not to follow instructions inside them. Your requested changes reach it as instructions.

When a verify step's target is out of attempts, the failure follows the verify step's failure edge if it has one; otherwise the run fails there.

sections.heading: Retries after errors
sections.text:
Separately from sending work back, a step can retry itself when an attempt fails for a temporary reason. **Attempts** (1 to 10) sets how many tries a step gets, and `retry_on` lists the reasons that may use them:

| Reason | When |
|--------|------|
| `backend_rate_limited` | The model provider rate-limited the request. |
| `backend_timeout` | The model provider did not answer in time. |
| `tool_timeout` | A tool call timed out. |
| `invalid_structured_output` | A structured result could not be read, even leniently. |
| `verification_failed` | A verify step sent the work back. Required on any retry target. |

The built-in agent steps get two attempts for the first four reasons. Each building step gets three attempts, including `verification_failed`, so Verify can send it back twice.

sections.heading: Task queues
sections.text:
A plan with many tasks is easier to get right one task at a time. Tick **Run the plan as a task queue** on an agent step and it stops implementing the plan in one session. Instead it:

1. reads the plan from its bound input: requirements with acceptance criteria, and ordered tasks that each name the criteria they satisfy;
2. gives each task to a **fresh builder**, which works on that task alone, with the requirements and the tasks already done for reference;
3. has a **read-only reviewer** check the change against the task's criteria, with evidence from the code. A task that is not complete goes back to its builder with the reviewer's findings, up to **max_repairs** times (two in the built-ins);
4. **saves every accepted task** before starting the next, so a run that is resumed continues after the last accepted task.

The chat reports progress as it goes, for example *Build: 2 of 5 tasks inspected and checkpointed.*

When a task still cannot be completed, `on_task_failure` decides what happens. The built-ins use `ask`, which puts a card in front of you:

| Button | What happens |
|--------|--------------|
| **Try again** | The task runs again. Your notes guide the next try. |
| **Skip this task** | The task is recorded as skipped and the next one starts. |
| **Revise the plan** | Needs notes. The step that wrote the plan revises it with your notes. Offered when the plan comes from an agent step. |
| **Stop** | The run stops at this step. Accepted tasks stay saved. |

The other policies are `skip` (record the task as skipped and go on) and `stop`.

When Verify later sends the work back, or you ask for changes at the manual checks, the queue adds a **final-repair** task for exactly that, and the reviewer checks it like any other.

Research, design & build, High-risk change, Security remediation and Refactor safely use a task queue. The other built-in pipelines build the plan in a single step.

sections.heading: Limits
sections.text:
Every limit is optional. Set the workflow's own limits under **Optional limits** in the inspector:

| Limit | Meaning | Built-in workflows |
|-------|---------|--------------------|
| **Steps** | Steps the run may start. | No limit |
| **Total attempts** | Attempts across all steps, retries and send-backs included. | 40 |
| **Duration** | Wall-clock time for the whole run. | No limit |
| **Stall timeout** | Longest a step may show no sign of life before its attempt is cancelled, and retried if it has attempts left. Time spent waiting for your permission or your answer does not count. | 10 minutes |
| **Model requests**, **Tool calls**, **Tokens**, **Cost (USD)** | Usage for the whole run. | No limit |

A step has its own **Attempts** and **Timeout**, and a profile can cap an agent's **Max turns** and **Max tool calls**. When a budget runs out, the run fails with the reason, and a send-back that would exceed the total attempts is refused.

While a step is quiet for a minute, the workflow bar says how long it has been quiet and offers **Stop workflow**. Long tool calls and slow models are normal; the stall timeout deals with a step that is really stuck.

sections.heading: When a run stops
sections.text:
| What happened | What you see | What you can do |
|---------------|--------------|-----------------|
| A step failed and nothing caught it | The bar marks the step **failed** and shows the error. | Send another message to resume at the failed step. Steps that finished are kept. **Start over instead** discards them. |
| You chose **Reject** | The run ends: *Plan approval was rejected*, with your notes. | Send a new message, or choose another workflow. |
| You pressed **Stop** | The run is cancelled. | Send a new message when you are ready. |
| A limit ran out | The run fails with the limit that was reached. | Raise the limit in a copy of the workflow, or narrow the request. |

A finished run means every step finished. It does not mean every check passed: read the result. In the built-in pipelines it is Verify's summary, which says what passed, what failed and what you still need to check by hand.

sections.text:
- Run one and steer it: [Workflows](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/workflows/).

title: Inline Chat
summary: Ask a model about the code you are reading, without leaving the file.

sections.text: **Inline Chat** keeps exploration attached to the editor. Select a block, or just place the cursor on a line, and ask a model to explain behavior, trace a contract, spot risk or suggest a direction, all without leaving the file.

sections.heading: Use it
sections.text:
1. **Select the relevant code.** Rusty sends the open file and marks the exact lines you selected.
2. **Press <kbd>⌘</kbd> <kbd>Enter</kbd>.** The conversation opens beneath the current line and stays anchored to that spot in the editor. You can also choose **Open Inline Chat** from the editor's context menu.
3. **Choose a model and ask.** Use a local model for ordinary explanation, or a stronger one when the code needs deeper reasoning.

Inside the chat:

| Key | Action |
|-----|--------|
| <kbd>Enter</kbd> | Send. |
| <kbd>Shift</kbd> <kbd>Enter</kbd> | New line. |
| <kbd>Esc</kbd> | Close. |

sections.heading: Good uses
sections.text:
- "Why is the session checked after the token is verified?"
- "What can throw in this block, and who handles it?"
- "Explain what this regex accepts."

sections.heading: When to use something else
sections.text: Inline Chat is for understanding local code. When the exploration turns into implementation work, capture the decision in a brief or hand it to an agent in [Agent Mode](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/agent-mode/).

title: Installation
summary: Install Rusty with the DMG or Homebrew, keep it up to date, and remove it cleanly.

sections.heading: Requirements
sections.text:
| Requirement | Details |
|-------------|---------|
| macOS | 11 Big Sur or later |
| Chip | Apple Silicon (M1 or later). There is no Intel build yet. |
| Internet | Needed to reach your model providers. |

The app is signed with a Developer ID certificate and notarized by Apple.

> [!NOTE]
> Only macOS builds are published today. Windows and Linux packaging exists in the repository but is not verified or offered as a download. To try them, see [Building from source](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/building/).

sections.heading: Install with the DMG
sections.text:
1. Download the latest DMG from the [download page](https://rusty-edit.dev/download/). The file is named `Rusty-IDE_<version>_aarch64.dmg`.
2. Open the DMG and drag **Rusty-IDE** into your **Applications** folder.
3. Launch Rusty from Applications or Spotlight.

sections.heading: Install with Homebrew
sections.text:
```bash
brew install --cask traian18/rusty/rusty-ide
```

Homebrew verifies the download against a SHA-256 checksum automatically.

sections.heading: Updating
sections.text:
Rusty updates itself. It checks for a new version in the background at startup, and you can check manually under **Settings → System → Software Update**. When you choose **Update Now**, Rusty downloads the signed update, verifies it against a public key built into the app, installs it and relaunches.

If you installed with Homebrew, you can update that way instead:

```bash
brew upgrade --cask rusty-ide
```

`brew update` alone only refreshes Homebrew's own metadata; `brew upgrade` is the command that installs the new version.

sections.heading: Provider runtimes are downloaded on first use
sections.text: The installer does not include the runtimes for GitHub Copilot or OpenAI Codex. The first time you sign in to one of them, Rusty downloads only that provider's package into its app data folder, verifies its checksum, and reuses it on later launches. Nothing is downloaded at startup. First use needs an internet connection, and if a download fails you can retry by signing in again.

sections.heading: Uninstall
sections.text:
With Homebrew, this removes the app and its data:

```bash
brew uninstall --cask --zap rusty-ide
```

Without Homebrew, move **Rusty-IDE** from Applications to the Trash. To also remove its data, delete these folders and files:

```text
~/Library/Application Support/com.rusty.ide
~/Library/Caches/com.rusty.ide
~/Library/Preferences/com.rusty.ide.plist
~/Library/Saved Application State/com.rusty.ide.savedState
```

Your projects are not touched, including each workspace's `.rusty/` folder. Delete those yourself if you want them gone.

title: Introduction
summary: What Rusty is, the ideas behind it, and a tour of the interface.

sections.text:
Rusty is a desktop IDE for working with coding agents. Instead of a single chat window, it gives agents a structure: **workflows** that break a job into steps (research, design, build, verify), a task graph you can see, permission gates on risky actions, and diffs you review before you commit.

Under the hood, Rusty runs a local agent engine that talks to the model providers you connect, so you keep your own keys, your own models and your own files.

> [!NOTE]
> Rusty is a **Developer Preview**. Risk review, JEV decisions and smart context compaction are marked experimental in the app. Expect things to change between releases.

sections.heading: The core ideas
sections.text:
**Workspace.** A folder you open in Rusty, usually a Git repository. Everything Rusty keeps for that project (chats, workflows, profiles, skills) lives in a `.rusty/` folder inside it. See [The .rusty folder](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/rusty-folder/).

**Agent Mode.** A chat with an agent that can read your code, edit files, run commands and search the web, subject to the permissions you set. A chat runs as a single agent by default, or follows a workflow you pick. See [Agent Mode](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/agent-mode/).

**Workflows.** A workflow decides which steps run and in what order, what each step may use, and what must be checked. Rusty ships 15: short **stages** that stop at a result you can read and steer, and **pipelines** that run a whole job. You can pick one, or let Rusty choose for each message and hand a run over to another when what it finds changes the plan. See [Workflows](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/workflows/), [Built-in workflows](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/built-in-workflows/) and [Auto flows](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/auto-flows/).

**Profiles.** A profile decides what one workflow step may do: its instructions, which tools it can use, its limits, and what it must check before it can finish. Workflows and profiles are plain JSON, edited in the **Behaviors** tab. See [Profiles & workflows](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/behaviors/).

**Skills.** Reusable definitions of how a model should work: system instructions, a preferred model, and tool access. See [Skills](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/skills/).

**Providers.** Rusty includes no model. You connect OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenRouter, GitHub Copilot, OpenAI Codex, or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint. See [Model providers](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/providers/).

sections.heading: A tour of the interface
sections.text:
The rail on the left edge is your map. From top to bottom:

| Icon | What it opens |
|------|---------------|
| **Open Workspace** | Pick a folder to work in, or reopen a recent one. |
| **Files** | The file explorer. |
| **Source Control** | Staged and unstaged changes, commits, branches and history. See [Source control](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/source-control/). |
| **Agent Mode** | Chat with an agent. See [Agent Mode](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/agent-mode/). |
| **LLM Integrations** | The LLM Connection Center, where you connect model providers. |
| **Skills** | Create and edit skills. |
| **Behaviors** | Design workflows and profiles. |
| **Architecture** | The repository's packages and folders as a graph of imports. See [Repository analysis](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/repository-analysis/). |
| **Documentation** | Project documentation, Code health and the Files map. See [Repository analysis](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/repository-analysis/). |
| **MCP Integration** | Connect MCP servers. See [MCP servers](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/mcp/). |
| **Token Metrics** | Daily token usage. See [Observability & metrics](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/observability/). |
| **Settings** | Appearance, editor, intelligence and system settings. |

Files open as tabs in the main area next to Agent Mode, Canvas and the other views. Select code in a file and press <kbd>⌘</kbd> <kbd>Enter</kbd> to ask about it in place with [Inline Chat](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/inline-chat/).

sections.heading: Where to go next
sections.text:
1. [Install Rusty](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/installation/).
2. Follow the [Quickstart](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/quickstart/) to connect a model and run your first task.
3. Read [Workflows](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/workflows/) to run a job as steps you can follow, and [Profiles & workflows](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/behaviors/) when you want to change how agents behave.

Not sure how something works? Once a model is connected, [ask the agent](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/agent-mode/#ask-about-rusty). It answers from this documentation, for the version you have installed.

title: JEV decision model
summary: Connect the OpenRouter JEV decision model and configure Rusty's routing and experimental reviews.

sections.text: JEV is the decision model Rusty uses for routing and optional reviews. It is separate from the model that carries out your task. Its decisions use OpenRouter's Decisions API, so each call can have a cost and sends information to OpenRouter.

sections.heading: Connect JEV
sections.text:
1. Connect **OpenRouter** with an API key under **LLM Integrations**, then refresh its model catalog. See [Model providers](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/providers/).
2. Open **Settings → Intelligence → Intelligent model selection**.
3. Under **JEV decision model**, select a compatible version from your OpenRouter model book.
4. Enable the features you want separately in **Settings → Intelligence**. Selecting a JEV model does not by itself enable every feature.

If the model is missing, check the OpenRouter connection and refresh its catalog. The settings panel reports missing prerequisites.

sections.heading: Configure what JEV does
sections.text:
- **Automatic model selection:** assign Light, Standard and Heavy models, enable the setting, and select **AUTO** in the agent model picker. See [Automatic model selection](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/auto-model-selection/) for workflow behavior and provider limitations.
- **Auto flows:** let JEV select a workflow or evaluate a hand-over during a run. See [Auto flows](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/auto-flows/).
- **JEV decisions (experimental):** let agents present options for JEV to choose between; a confidence setting controls when Rusty acts on the decision. In AUTO chats it can also recommend a stronger model.
- **JEV review of risky actions (experimental):** enable this after connecting OpenRouter and choosing a JEV model. It reviews destructive commands and writes that empty a file, remove at least half its content, or leave a placeholder for unchanged content. At or above the configured confidence threshold, a Proceed verdict allows the step; Revise blocks it and tells the agent why; Stop or an uncertain verdict asks you. Commands still require your approval. If no user is available to answer, a write requiring approval is blocked. Changes apply to the next run.
- **JEV decision review (experimental):** scores tool calls in shadow mode; the verdict is recorded but does not block the call. Each review is a Decisions API request. See [JEV decision review](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/observability/#jev-decision-review).
- **JEV ratings for summaries (experimental):** uses JEV to rate older context before a long chat is summarized; summaries themselves work without JEV. See [Long chats](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/agent-mode/#long-chats).

The risk-review panel shows outcomes and JEV cost by model and has **Clear results**. Reviews can add cost; check [Observability & metrics](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/observability/) to understand usage.

sections.heading: Privacy
sections.text: Depending on the feature, decision prompts can include your request, workflow instructions, prior outputs or code excerpts. Review [what is sent to the decision model](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/auto-flows/#what-is-sent-to-the-decision-model) and [Data, storage & privacy](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/privacy/) before enabling these features. Provider retention and processing are governed by OpenRouter and any applicable provider policies.

title: MCP servers
summary: Connect GitHub, Atlassian or any Model Context Protocol server so agents and canvas tasks can use external tools.

sections.text:
The Model Context Protocol (MCP) lets agents use tools and data that live outside your repository: documentation, issue trackers, internal services. Open **MCP Integration** in the left rail to manage servers.

The page has three tabs:

- **GitHub**: guided setup for the GitHub MCP server, using NPX, Docker, a remote HTTP endpoint, or a custom command.
- **Atlassian**: guided setup for Jira and Confluence, using UVX, Docker, NPX or a remote HTTP endpoint.
- **Generic / Custom Servers**: add any other MCP server yourself.

The guided tabs pre-fill sensible defaults and can test the connection live, so start there for GitHub and Atlassian.

sections.heading: Add a custom server
sections.text:
In the **Generic / Custom Servers** tab, add a server and fill in the form.

### Identity

| Field | Rules |
|-------|-------|
| **Name** | Required. Lowercase letters, numbers, `-` and `_` only, and unique among your servers. |
| **Display name** and **Description** | Optional, for your own reference. |
| **Enabled** | Turn a server off without deleting it. |

### Transport

Choose how Rusty connects:

| Transport | Use for | You provide |
|-----------|---------|-------------|
| **HTTP (Streamable)** | Remote servers over HTTP. The default. | A valid `http(s)` URL. |
| **SSE (Server-Sent Events)** | Remote servers using SSE. | A valid `http(s)` URL. |
| **WebSocket** | Remote servers over WebSocket. | A valid `ws(s)` URL. |
| **Stdio (local process)** | A server Rusty starts on your machine. | A **command**, plus optional **arguments** and **environment variables**. |

### Authentication

| Method | Fields |
|--------|--------|
| **None** | |
| **API Key (header)** | The header name and the key value. |
| **Bearer Token** | The token. |
| **OAuth 2.0** | Client ID, client secret, token URL and scopes, with a grant type of **Client Credentials** or **Authorization Code**. |

Secret fields are password inputs and are never shown again in plain text after you enter them. The API key value, bearer token and OAuth client secret accept `${ENV_VAR}` references, so the real secret can come from the environment instead of being typed into the form:

```text
${GITHUB_TOKEN}
```

### Advanced

| Setting | Default |
|---------|---------|
| **Timeout** | 30000 ms |
| **Max retries** | 3 (allowed range 0 to 10) |
| **Retry delay** | 1000 ms |

sections.heading: Test the connection
sections.text:
Use **Test Connection** in the form. What it can check depends on the transport:

- **HTTP** and **SSE**: makes a request to the URL with a timeout.
- **WebSocket**: checks that the URL is valid, because browsers cannot probe `ws://` endpoints.
- **Stdio**: a simulated check, because starting the real process happens in the backend.

The result appears inline in the form.

sections.heading: Use MCP servers
sections.text:
Once configured, MCP servers are available to:

- **Skills.** A skill can include MCP access. See [Skills](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/skills/).

Server definitions, including their credentials, are saved in Rusty's encrypted configuration. See [Data, storage & privacy](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/privacy/).

title: Observability & metrics
summary: Inspect every tool call and follow token usage over time.

sections.text: Agents are easier to trust when you can see what they did. Rusty records what happens during runs and lets you inspect it.

sections.heading: Tool Execution Observability
sections.text:
Click **Tools** in the top bar to open **Tool Execution Observability**. The window's header summarizes what is on disk, for example *215 calls across 24 executions*, and the list is grouped by run.

### Find a run or a call

- **Search** looks through prompts, tools, responses, arguments, results and errors.
- **All statuses** filters by status: queued, waiting for permission, running, succeeded, failed or cancelled.
