- **All sources** filters by the source of a run, such as `agent_chat`.

### Read a run

Each run is a card showing the prompt that started it, where it came from (for example `agent_chat`), the model it used, the time, the number of calls, how long it took and the tokens it used. Inside, a timeline lays out the run step by step: each assistant turn and each tool call, with its time offset from the start of the run. Expand **Event Trace** under a run to see its raw events.

Select a call in the timeline to see its details on the right:

| Section | What it shows |
|---------|---------------|
| **Call Output** | The result the tool returned, with a **Copy result** button. |
| **Tool Execution** | Which **model executed** the call and its **provider**, then a timestamped trace of the steps. |
| **Run Context (Initiating Prompt)** | The user request that started the run, with **Copy prompt**. Every call in a run shares it. |
| **Run Token Usage** | Tokens by model: input, output, cache read, cache write and total. |
| **Call Metadata** | Details about the call, such as its source and surface. |

### Who ran each call

[Smart tools](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/smart-tools/) hand their reading to a separate selector model. For those calls, **Tool Execution** names the selector as the executor, along with its provider and a purpose such as *Smart Read selector*. The trace shows each step of the selection: the file loaded for the selector, the selector invocation starting and completing, and the ranges it selected. The selector's tokens are tracked separately from the main run's.

The same view records decisions made by the decision model (JEV). An [automatic model selection](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/auto-model-selection/) decision appears as a `jev_model_selection` call in the timeline, with the model that made it.

### Flow decisions

When [Auto flows](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/auto-flows/) choose a workflow for a message, or check whether a running workflow should hand over, each decision is recorded as its own run with one call. A choice appears as **AUTO flow selection**, and a boundary check as **AUTO flow switching · *workflow***. Open one to see the request sent to the decision model, the option it chose with its confidence, the ranked probabilities, what the decision cost, and, if it failed, why. The steps read *Asked … which workflow fits the message* or *Asked … whether "…" should carry on or hand over*.

With [automatic model selection](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/auto-model-selection/#workflows-a-model-for-each-step) on a workflow, each step's model choice is recorded the same way, labelled **AUTO model selection · *step***.

### JEV decision review

If you turn on **JEV decision review (experimental)** under **Settings → Intelligence**, JEV scores every tool call as **Proceed**, **Revise** or **Stop**. It runs in shadow mode: the call always runs, and the verdict is recorded on the call. In the trace it appears as a line such as *JEV shadow: Revise with confidence 0.34. Not enforced.* Each scored call is one Decisions API request to your OpenRouter decision model.

### The footer

The bottom of the window shows **History on disk**: how many calls and runs are shown, the folder they live in (`.rusty/observability`) and its size. **All-time tokens** totals your usage by type. Use **Show** to choose how far back to list, such as 30 days, and **Clear history** to delete the records.

Records are stored locally in your workspace. Rusty adds a `.gitignore` there so they are not committed by accident. See [The .rusty folder](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/rusty-folder/).

sections.heading: Token Metrics
sections.text:
Open **Token Metrics** in the left rail to follow usage. The rail icon also shows today's total, in compact form, so you can watch it as you work.

Choose a period at the top of the tab:

| Period |
|--------|
| Today |
| Yesterday |
| 7 days |
| 30 days |
| All time |
| Custom |

Use it to see how your model choices add up. For instance, whether [automatic model selection](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/auto-model-selection/) is keeping routine work on your cheaper models.

Metrics are kept locally in `.rusty/metrics/`, which is also excluded from Git automatically.

title: Permissions & safety
summary: How Rusty asks before running commands, and the tool limits and rules that keep agents in bounds.

sections.text: Agents act on your real files and can run commands with your credentials, so Rusty puts several layers between an agent and a risky action. Each layer is independent, so you can combine them.

sections.heading: Command permission prompts
sections.text:
When an agent wants to run a shell command, Rusty stops and shows **Command permission required**. The prompt tells you:

- **The command**, with its arguments.
- **A risk badge**: `elevated` or `destructive`. Destructive commands carry an extra warning, because they may modify infrastructure, remote systems or project state.
- **The working directory** the command will run in.
- **The timeout**, in seconds.

The command runs against your real workspace files, in the IDE's own environment, and may use any local or cloud credentials you have configured. Read it before you approve.

You have three choices:

| Button | Effect |
|--------|--------|
| **Deny** | The command is refused, and the agent is told so. |
| **Allow once** | Runs this one command. |
| **Allow *program* this session** | Allows other normal-risk commands from the same program for the rest of this agent session. When a command cannot be safely grouped by program, the button reads **Allow exact command this session** and applies only to that exact command. |

Session grants are held in memory only. They end with the agent session and are never saved. Elevated or destructive variants of an allowed program still ask again, and changing an exact command's arguments asks again.

sections.heading: Tool allow-lists
sections.text:
A [profile](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/behaviors/#profiles) can restrict a workflow step to a named set of tools. The built-in **Plan** step is limited to reading and searching tools, so it cannot edit files or run commands at all:

```json
"tools": {
  "type": "allow_list",
  "tools": ["read_file", "list_files", "search_codebase", "web_search", "web_extract", "report_progress", "ask_user_question"]
}
```

sections.heading: Read-only workflows and Auto
sections.text:
The built-in workflows use these tool limits on purpose. Research, Analyze, Plan, Architect, Security and Review cannot write files or run commands, and Debug and Verify cannot write files, so a stage such as **Research & analyze** or **Verify & review changes** cannot change your project. Only Build, Refactor, Optimize and Document steps can. See [Built-in workflows](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/built-in-workflows/#built-in-profiles).

When [Auto flows](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/auto-flows/) choose a workflow for you, they never start one that can change files without asking first, and they ask again before handing a running workflow over to one. Command permission prompts apply inside every workflow.

sections.heading: Rules
Completion gates
sections.text: A [completion gate](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/behaviors/#completion-gates) prevents a step from finishing until required checks are met. The built-in **Build** step cannot report until it has verified its own edits.

sections.heading: Risk review (experimental)
sections.text: Before an agent destructively overwrites a file or runs a destructive command, the decision model can review the step. It can let the step run, send the agent back to revise, or ask you. The settings panel keeps counts of what it allowed, blocked and sent back. This needs OpenRouter connected with a decision model chosen. See [Automatic model selection](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/auto-model-selection/#related-experimental-features).

sections.heading: Review before you commit
sections.text: Whatever the agent did, Git is your last checkpoint. Look at the diff in [Source control](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/source-control/) before you commit.

title: Data, storage & privacy
summary: Where Rusty keeps your keys, chats and settings, and where your requests go.

sections.text: Rusty runs on your machine. This page explains what it stores and where your data goes.

sections.heading: Where requests go
sections.text:
Model requests go to the providers you connect, using the keys or sign-ins you give Rusty. If you use a local OpenAI-compatible server, model requests stay on your machine.

Some features call other services you configure: [web search providers](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/smart-tools/#web-search-providers), [MCP servers](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/mcp/) and the selector models behind [smart tools](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/smart-tools/). Each is opt-in and uses the provider or server you choose.

Rusty also contacts GitHub to check for updates, as described in [Installation](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/installation/#updating).

### The decision model

[Automatic model selection](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/auto-model-selection/) and [Auto flows](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/auto-flows/) send short prompts to the **OpenRouter Decisions API**, with your OpenRouter key. Model selection sends your request (clipped to a fixed length). Choosing a workflow sends your message and an excerpt of the last result. A [hand-over check](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/auto-flows/#hand-over-mid-run) sends your request and the outputs of the workflow steps finished so far, which can quote your code. [What is sent](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/auto-flows/#what-is-sent-to-the-decision-model) lists the limits. None of this goes to the provider of the model that does your work, and none of it happens unless you have chosen to use these features.

sections.heading: Provider keys and MCP credentials
sections.text:
API keys, tokens and MCP server settings are saved in Rusty's application configuration, encrypted with **AES-GCM**. The encryption key is a random 256-bit key held in the **macOS Keychain**. If no keychain is available, it is kept in an owner-only file in the app's data folder instead. The key is never shipped inside the app.

Two safeguards protect against data loss:

- If the key cannot be obtained at all, for example because the keychain is locked, Rusty does not save anything over your existing configuration during that session.
- If the key is available but cannot decrypt the stored data, for example because the keychain entry was reset, Rusty moves the old data aside under a backup key and starts fresh instead of overwriting it.

Sign-ins for **GitHub Copilot** and **OpenAI Codex** are handled by those providers' own tooling. Rusty does not store their OAuth tokens in its provider settings. Codex credentials live in `~/.codex`, shared with the Codex CLI and desktop app.

**Settings → System → Storage & Cache** tells you which is in use: it reports that secrets are encrypted with a key held in the OS keychain, or that the keychain was unavailable and an owner-only file is used instead. It also warns you if previously saved secrets could not be decrypted, in which case you need to re-enter your tokens.

sections.heading: Secret Shield
sections.text:
Under **Settings → Intelligence → Secrets Shield**, choose how Rusty handles credential patterns in outbound model requests. Detection runs locally over text and structured tool data before a model receives the request:

| Policy | Behavior |
|--------|----------|
| **Off** | Send requests unchanged. |
| **Warn** | Log a warning and send unchanged. |
| **Mask** | Replace matches with `[REDACTED]`. This is the default. |
| **Block** | Do not send requests containing matches. |

Detection is pattern-based: it can miss secrets or match ordinary text, and it does not scan image contents. It is not a guarantee that a request contains no sensitive data. Secret Shield controls outbound model requests only; it does not redact local chat history or diagnostics, or replace care when sharing files and logs.

sections.heading: Project data
sections.text: Chats, workflows, profiles, skills, metrics and observability records are plain files in the workspace's `.rusty/` folder. Chats can contain messages and information about modified files; observability can contain tool execution records and diagnostics. These files are not protected by Secret Shield's outbound masking. Review them before sharing or committing them. See [The .rusty folder](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/rusty-folder/) for the folder-by-folder breakdown and Git guidance. Deleting a folder there removes the data in it.

sections.heading: Application data on your Mac
sections.text:
Rusty stores its own settings and caches in these locations:

```text
~/Library/Application Support/com.rusty.ide
~/Library/Caches/com.rusty.ide
~/Library/Preferences/com.rusty.ide.plist
~/Library/Saved Application State/com.rusty.ide.savedState
```

[Repository analysis](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/repository-analysis/) results and written project documentation are saved in the `repositories` and `documentation` folders under `~/Library/Application Support/com.rusty.ide`, not in your workspace. The analysis itself uses no model and sends nothing anywhere; writing documentation pages sends their briefs and code excerpts to the model you pick.

Under **Settings → System → Storage & Cache**, **Application Cache & Logs** shows how much space the WebView cache, process logs and local execution telemetry take up. **Delete Cache** clears them. It does not affect your workspaces, project files or settings.

sections.heading: Commands and files
sections.text: Agents work on your real files and can run commands in the IDE's own environment, which may include the credentials in your shell environment and tools. Rusty asks before it runs commands. See [Permissions & safety](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/permissions/).

sections.heading: This website
sections.text: The Rusty website sets no cookies and runs no analytics. The download button asks GitHub's public API for the latest release when the page loads, and the file itself downloads directly from GitHub.

title: Model providers
summary: Connect OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenRouter, GitHub Copilot, OpenAI Codex or any OpenAI-compatible server.

sections.text: Rusty does not include a model. You connect the providers you already use in the **LLM Connection Center**, opened from **LLM Integrations** in the left rail. Requests go directly to the providers you configure.

sections.heading: Built-in providers
sections.text:
| Provider | How you connect | Notes |
|----------|-----------------|-------|
| **OpenAI** | API key | Connects directly to OpenAI. If the key is blank, Rusty falls back to the `OPENAI_API_KEY` environment variable. |
| **Anthropic** | API key | Connects directly to Anthropic's Claude API. Falls back to `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` if the key is blank. |
| **OpenRouter** | API key | A unified OpenAI-compatible gateway to many providers. Falls back to `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`. Use **Fetch Models** to discover what is available. Required for [automatic model selection](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/auto-model-selection/). |
| **GitHub Models** | Personal access token | Uses GitHub's OpenAI-compatible inference API. Needs a token with the `models:read` scope, or `GITHUB_TOKEN`. |
| **GitHub Copilot** | Sign-in | Uses your Copilot subscription through GitHub's official Copilot SDK. Available models and premium-request usage depend on your plan and organization policy. |
| **OpenAI Codex** | Sign-in | Uses your existing OpenAI Codex sign-in through the official Codex app-server. Credentials are shared with the Codex CLI and desktop app through `~/.codex`. Available models come from your account. |
| **OpenCode Zen** | API key | Connects to OpenCode Zen and uses `OPENCODE_API_KEY` if the key is blank. To use OpenCode Go, register it separately as `opencode-go` with its own base URL. |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Claude models are reached with an **Anthropic API key**. Signing in with a Claude subscription is not supported.

sections.heading: Connect a provider with an API key
sections.text:
1. Open **LLM Integrations**.
2. Select the provider in the list. Its **Provider Configuration** panel opens.
3. Fill in the fields:

   | Field | What it is |
   |-------|-----------|
   | **API Authorization Key** | Your key or token. It is stored encrypted, see [Data, storage & privacy](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/privacy/). |
   | **Connection Base URL** | The API endpoint, for example `https://api.openai.com/v1`. Pre-filled for built-in providers. |
   | **Model Catalog URL** | Where Rusty lists models. Defaults to the base URL plus `/models`. |
   | **Default API Protocol** | How Rusty talks to the API. See below. |
   | **Default Target Model** | The model used when none is chosen explicitly. |

4. Click **Save Configuration**.
5. Fetch the model catalog so the provider's models show up in the model pickers.

sections.heading: Sign in with GitHub Copilot or OpenAI Codex
sections.text:
These two providers use your existing subscription instead of an API key.

1. Select **GitHub Copilot** or **OpenAI Codex** in the list.
2. Click **Sign in with GitHub Copilot** (or **Sign in with OpenAI Codex**).
3. Complete the sign-in. Rusty either opens a browser window for you, or shows a **device code**: use **Copy Code**, then open the verification page and enter it.
4. When it reads **Connected**, the models your account can use appear in the pickers.

Use **Cancel** to abandon a sign-in in progress, **Re-authenticate** to sign in again, and **Sign out** to disconnect.

Rusty never stores the OAuth token in its own provider settings. The official Codex app-server keeps Codex credentials in `~/.codex`, and the Copilot CLI uses the system credential store.

The first time you sign in, Rusty downloads that provider's runtime, since installers do not include it. See [Installation](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/installation/#provider-runtimes-are-downloaded-on-first-use). If something goes wrong, expand **Authentication diagnostics** and use **Copy Diagnostics** to copy details you can share.

sections.heading: Add a custom or local provider
sections.text:
Any server that speaks an OpenAI-compatible API works, including Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM and LiteLLM gateways.

1. In the LLM Connection Center, choose **Register Custom LLM / Local Host** (**New Custom Provider**).
2. Fill in the form:

   | Field | Example |
   |-------|---------|
   | **Provider ID** | `ollama` |
   | **Display Name** | `Local Ollama Runner` |
   | **Base API URL** | `http://localhost:11434/v1` |
   | **Catalog URL** *(optional)* | Defaults to `{base URL}/models` |
   | **API Protocol** | See below |
   | **Authentication** | See below |
   | **Models** *(comma-separated)* | `qwen2.5-coder:7b, llama3.3:70b` |

3. Click **Register Provider**.

### API protocols

| Option | Use it for |
|--------|-----------|
| **OpenAI Chat Completions** | Most OpenAI-compatible servers: Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM, LiteLLM, OpenRouter. |
| **OpenAI Responses** | Endpoints that implement OpenAI's Responses API. |
| **Anthropic Messages** | Anthropic's API or a compatible gateway. |
| **Google Generative AI** | Google's Gemini API. |

### Authentication

| Option | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **None / Local** | No credentials, for example a local server. |
| **Bearer token** | Sends your key as `Authorization: Bearer …`. |
| **Anthropic x-api-key** | Sends your key in Anthropic's `x-api-key` header. |

sections.heading: Reasoning effort variants
sections.text: For models that support it, Rusty lists reasoning-effort variants of the same model: **Minimal**, **Low**, **Medium**, **High** and **Extra High**. Pick a variant in the model picker like any other model, and use them when you [map models to AUTO levels](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/auto-model-selection/).

sections.heading: Environment variables
sections.text: Where a provider says it falls back to an environment variable, that variable is read from the environment Rusty was launched with. Apps started from Finder or the Dock do not inherit variables you export in your shell profile, so paste the key into the provider's configuration instead.

title: Quickstart
summary: Connect a model, open a workspace, and run your first task in about five minutes.

sections.text: This walks you from a fresh install to a reviewed change.

sections.heading: 1. Connect a model
sections.text:
Rusty needs at least one model provider.

1. Click **LLM Integrations** in the left rail to open the **LLM Connection Center**.
2. Choose a provider from the list: OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenRouter and others.
3. Paste your **API Authorization Key**.
4. Click **Save Configuration**, then fetch the provider's model catalog so its models appear in pickers.

No key handy? You can sign in with an existing **GitHub Copilot** or **OpenAI Codex** subscription instead, or point Rusty at a local OpenAI-compatible server such as Ollama. All of these are covered in [Model providers](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/providers/).

sections.heading: 2. Open a workspace
sections.text: Click **Open Workspace** and choose the folder of a project, ideally one that is a Git repository so you can review changes with [source control](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/source-control/). Rusty creates a `.rusty/` folder there for chats, workflows and other project data.

sections.heading: 3. Run your first task
sections.text:
1. Click **Agent Mode**.
2. Pick a model in the model picker. If you have set up [automatic model selection](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/auto-model-selection/), you can choose **AUTO** instead.
3. Above the message box, the **Mode** menu shows what the chat will follow. New chats start as a **Single agent**, one agent loop that suits a quick answer or a small edit. For a bigger job, choose a workflow such as **Plan, build, verify**, or a stage such as **Research & analyze** if you want to read the findings before anything is built. With OpenRouter connected you can also choose **Auto** and let Rusty pick. See [Workflows](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/workflows/).
4. Describe the task in the message box. Type `@` to reference a file.

While the agent works you will see each step's progress, and every tool call it makes. When it wants to run a shell command, Rusty asks first:

- **Deny** refuses the command.
- **Allow once** runs just this command.
- **Allow this session** allows the program (or the exact command) for the rest of this agent session, in memory only.

See [Permissions & safety](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/permissions/) for how these prompts work.

sections.heading: 4. Review and commit
sections.text: Open **Source Control** to see what changed. Open a file's diff, stage what you want, write a commit message and press <kbd>⌘</kbd> <kbd>Enter</kbd> to commit.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text:
- Learn the [workflows](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/workflows/) that ship with Rusty, and how to [steer a long job between stages](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/workflows/#steer-a-long-job-between-stages).
- Make one of your own: [Your first workflow](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/first-workflow/).
- Let Rusty choose the workflow with [Auto flows](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/auto-flows/).
- Tune how agents behave in [Profiles & workflows](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/behaviors/).
- Give agents better context with [Smart tools](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/smart-tools/) and [MCP servers](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/mcp/).
- [Ask the agent](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/agent-mode/#ask-about-rusty) how any part of Rusty works, or where a setting lives.

title: Repository analysis
summary: The Architecture and Documentation tabs, code health scores, the Files map, and the repository tools agents use.

sections.text:
Rusty analyzes the repositories in your workspace: how files import each other, which framework routes and components connect them, how the code has changed in Git, and how complex each file is. The analysis runs on your machine, reads files without running or building anything, and uses no model. You can browse the results in two tabs, and agents can query the same data while they work.

Which languages and frameworks are covered is listed in [Supported languages & frameworks](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/supported-languages/).

sections.heading: Where to find it
sections.text:
Two entries on the left rail open the views:

- **Architecture** shows the repository as a graph of packages, folders and files.
- **Documentation** has three pages: **Project documentation**, **Code health** and **Files**.

When the workspace contains more than one repository, pick one with the selector at the top of either tab. The selection is shared with the Source Control sidebar.

The first analysis of a repository runs in the background. Running work appears in a small bubble at the bottom left, with a **×** to cancel each job. Results are saved, so reopening a tab or restarting Rusty does not start over, and unfinished work resumes after a restart.

sections.heading: Architecture
sections.text:
The summary strip at the top counts packages, files, imports, import cycles, languages and findings, and links the most important findings. Below it, each package is a bubble sized by the number of its files, and the lines between bubbles are imports, wider for more imports. A dashed line is an import used only for types, and a red line is part of an import cycle.

Double-click a group to open its folders, and keep going down to the files. The path at the top takes you back up.

| Control | What it does |
|---------|--------------|
| **Colour by** | **Each package** (its own colour), **Language**, **Kind**, or **Findings severity**. |
| **Edges** | The share of import weight drawn. Lower it to hide weaker lines in a busy graph. |
| **Spacing** | The distance between nodes. |
| **Imports** | **All**, **Runtime only**, or **Type-only** imports. |
| **Filter groups** | Show only groups whose name matches. |
| **With findings** | Show only groups that have findings. |
| **Refresh** | Analyze the repository again now. |

The panel on the right has three tabs. **Inspector** explains the selected node: why the group exists, its findings, and the imports that cross its boundary. **Findings** lists everything the analysis flagged in the current view. **Notes** holds your own notes on files and groups, kept on this computer and never in the repository.

Less connected nodes are folded into a single **+N more** bubble, and the bottom of the canvas says how many nodes and weaker lines are hidden.

### Findings

Findings are structural issues read from the import graph and Git history, such as import cycles, imports that cross a declared boundary, files that nothing imports, dependencies that are declared but not used (or used but not declared), tightly coupled files, and hotspots that change often. Each finding lists the files and lines involved. Findings are ranked by kind and size, not given a score.

sections.heading: Code health
sections.text:
Code health gives every file a score from 0 to 10. Each file starts at 10 and loses points for what the detectors find, with a cap per kind of issue so that no single issue dominates. No model is used, and every point lost comes with its evidence and line range.

The detectors look at three things:

- **The code itself:** complex or long functions, deep nesting, complex conditionals, functions with several separate complex sections, functions that are both long and complex, classes that do too much or whose methods share no state, and long lists of primitive parameters.
- **How it handles failure, duplication and tests:** errors that are caught and ignored (empty or catch-all handlers, results thrown away), functions that abort instead of returning an error (`unwrap`, `panic!`, `!!`, `printStackTrace`), functions copied almost unchanged to other places (renamed copies count), sizeable files that no test imports or is named after, tests that assert nothing, and several skipped tests in one file. Test code is judged by its own detectors and is not held to the error-handling and duplication rules.
- **Its change history** (when Git history is available): files that change often and are complex, files whose changes are spread across many places, files that are usually changed together with many others, files with many bug-fix commits, files owned mostly by one person or by someone no longer active, and files many people change at once. History can lower a score only so far, and less for code that is otherwise well structured.

The repository score is the average of file scores weighted by lines of code. Scores fall into five bands:

| Band | Score |
|------|-------|
| Excellent | 8.5 and above |
| Good | 7.0 to 8.5 |
| Fair | 5.5 to 7.0 |
| Needs work | 4.0 to 5.5 |
| At risk | under 4.0 |

Infrastructure files are scored the same way: Terraform, Terragrunt, CI pipelines, Dockerfiles, Compose files, Kubernetes manifests, Ansible, shell scripts and Makefiles, plus repository files such as `.gitignore` and `CODEOWNERS`. Their findings cover pinning (providers, modules, actions and images), security exposure (open ingress, broad permissions, secrets written into files), hygiene, and relations across files, such as Terragrunt dependency loops or Terraform variables nothing reads. [Supported languages & frameworks](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/supported-languages/#infrastructure-and-devops-files) lists what is checked for each kind. Findings about security count in their own category of the score.

Next to the score, the page shows maintainability (how hard the code is to change), the health of hotspots (the files that change most), the number of open issues, the lowest-scoring file, the share of files scored, and how many points were lost to the code itself versus its change history. **How scores work** explains the calculation. **Self-check** compares the lowest-scoring files with the files that were actually bug-fixed recently, so you can see whether the score points at the right files in your repository. It needs at least 25 scored files with history, 5 of them bug-fixed.

The tabs below the distribution bar show the same results four ways: **Files** (worst first), **Issues**, **Folders**, and **Map**. **Include tests** adds or removes test files. Click a file to open its details, with each issue, where it is, and a **Copy prompt** button that copies instructions for fixing it, ready to paste into a chat.

### Trend

Under the distribution bar, **Trend** shows a line of maintainability over time, the change since the previous analysis and since about 30 days earlier, and the files that fell the most since the last analysis. A point is recorded after every analysis; several analyses within ten minutes count as one point.

**Build history** re-scores up to 30 past commits, spread over the last two years, straight from Git's stored files without checking anything out, so the trend starts from the beginning. It runs as a background job in the process bubble and can be cancelled. Rebuilt points use maintainability, which counts only what the code shows (shape, duplication, error handling), so they compare with today's. They have no change-history findings or test links, because those need information that no longer exists for an old commit. Infrastructure files are not part of the trend.

sections.heading: Files
sections.text:
The Files page draws every file as a tile, grouped by folder and sized by lines of code (or switch **Size**). The lenses change what the colour means:

| Lens | Colour shows |
|------|--------------|
| **Language** | The language with the most lines in each tile. |
| **Churn** | Commits in the analyzed history; darker changed more. |
| **Dependents** | How many files import the most-imported file in the tile, as a percentile. |
| **Findings** | The most severe open finding in the tile. |
| **Owner** | Files where one person made 80% or more of the changes. |

The table below lists files with their language, lines, how many files import them, commits, main author and findings. Filter it by path, language and time range, show only files with findings, or hide tests.

sections.heading: Project documentation
sections.text:
**Project documentation** turns the analysis into pages you can read: an overview, getting started, key concepts, how it works, architecture, the active landscape, a glossary, and a page per top-level module. A model writes each page from a brief that Rusty builds out of the analysis, the README and excerpts of the code, and Rusty checks that the file paths and names the page mentions exist.

- **Written by** picks the model. By default it is your chat model.
- **Write documentation** writes every page that is missing or out of date. Before it starts, it shows the number of pages and an estimate of the input tokens; each page is one model call.
- **Write this page** writes only the page you are looking at.

The glossary is collected from the repository's own documents and is not written by a model. Pages are marked when the code they describe has changed since they were written. After a commit, Rusty asks whether to update the affected pages.

Two switches in the tab header control what happens in the background:

- **Index in background** analyzes the code again a few seconds after files change. Only changed files are measured again. No model is used.
- **Use in chats** adds the documentation pages that match a request to that chat's context.

sections.heading: Tools for agents
sections.text:
Agents can use the same analysis through read-only tools, available in Agent Mode, in every workflow step and on the Canvas:

| Tool | What the agent gets |
|------|---------------------|
| `repo_overview` | The shape of an unfamiliar repository: the written overview, packages and their heaviest dependencies, entry points, the most depended-on files, code health, infrastructure files by kind with their Terraform modules and Terragrunt units, hotspots and where to start reading. |
| `repo_context` | A file's connections: what it imports, what imports it, what changing it may affect, and recent changes. |
| `repo_symbol` | One function, method or class, instead of the whole file. |
| `repo_risk` | Before editing: how risky a change to these files is, and which tests to run. |
| `repo_health` | After editing: the files' health scores and issues, or the repository's biggest issues when asked what to improve. It also reports the maintainability trend, so an agent can tell whether the last change helped. |
| `code_guidelines` | The project's own [code guidelines](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/code-guidelines): what applies to a file before editing it, and what an edit broke of them. |
| `repo_wiki` | The project documentation pages. |

When a language is not supported, these tools say so instead of returning an error, so the agent can fall back to reading files. Calls appear in [Tool Execution Observability](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/observability/) like any other tool.

sections.heading: Where the results are stored
sections.text: The analysis and documentation pages are saved in Rusty's application data, not in your workspace, so they never show up in Git. Nothing is sent anywhere while analysing. A model only sees analysis results or documentation when you write pages, when **Use in chats** adds pages to a chat, or when an agent calls one of the tools above.

title: The .rusty folder
summary: What Rusty stores in each workspace, and what to commit.

sections.text:
Rusty keeps a project's data in a `.rusty/` folder at the root of the workspace. Most of it is plain JSON you can read, diff and share.

```text
your-project/
└── .rusty/
    ├── profiles/        behavior profiles       (commit)
    ├── workflows/       workflow definitions    (commit)
    ├── skills/          your skills             (commit)
    ├── chats/           Agent Mode conversations (your call)
    ├── observability/   tool execution records  (git-ignored automatically)
    └── metrics/         token usage             (git-ignored automatically)
```

sections.heading: What each folder holds
sections.text:
| Folder | Contents |
|--------|----------|
| `profiles/` | One JSON file per behavior profile: `<id>.json`. See [Profiles & workflows](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/behaviors/). |
| `workflows/` | One JSON file per workflow: `<id>.json`. The built-in workflows are part of the app and are not stored here; only workflows you write or customize are. |
| `skills/` | One JSON file per skill you create: `<id>.json`. See [Skills](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/skills/). |
| `chats/` | One file per Agent Mode conversation, with its messages and the files it modified. |
| `observability/` | Local records of tool executions, diagnostics and run trajectories. See [Observability & metrics](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/observability/). |
| `metrics/` | Token usage events and summaries for [Token Metrics](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/observability/#token-metrics). |

sections.heading: What to commit
sections.text:
Share the files that define **how agents behave** so your whole team gets the same setup:

- `.rusty/profiles/`
- `.rusty/workflows/`
- `.rusty/skills/`

Rusty writes a `.gitignore` containing `*` inside `observability/` and `metrics/`, so those stay out of version control without any setup.

Chats are personal working state and can be large. Whether to commit them is up to you; add `.rusty/chats/` to your `.gitignore` if you would rather not.

sections.heading: What is not stored here
sections.text: Provider API keys and MCP server credentials are **not** in `.rusty/`. They live in Rusty's encrypted application configuration. See [Data, storage & privacy](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/privacy/).

sections.heading: Editing files by hand
sections.text: Profiles and workflows are ordinary JSON, and the Behaviors editor keeps any fields it does not know about, so hand edits and editor edits coexist. A file with validation problems is flagged in the editor.

title: Skills
summary: Define how a model should work once, then apply it consistently in chats.

sections.text: A skill defines how a model works: its system instructions, its preferred model, and the tools and MCP access it should have. Configure it once in the **Skills** tab and apply it wherever you start work.

sections.heading: Built-in skills
sections.text:
Rusty ships with these:

| Skill | Purpose |
|-------|---------|
| **build** | Implement features, write clean code and run tests. Action-oriented. This is the default for new Agent chats. |
| **workflow-author** | In **Single agent** chat, design a workflow with you, review existing ones and suggest fixes, and save complete, validated workflows. Never runs them. |
| **plan** | Analyze architecture, explore code and propose plans. Read-only focus. |
| **grind-me** | Ask many clarifying questions before doing anything, and understand requirements thoroughly first. |
| **task-auditor** | Analyze tasks and suggest changes, approaches and execution plans. Does not write code. |

sections.heading: Workflow Author skill: create a workflow by describing it
sections.text:
The **workflow-author** skill builds a [workflow](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/workflows/) from a description, so you don't have to draw the graph yourself in the [Workflow Editor](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/workflow-editor/). It can also change a workflow you already have.

1. Open an Agent chat in **Single agent** mode.
2. In the skill picker, choose **workflow-author**.
3. Describe the workflow in plain words: what it starts from, the steps, who checks the work, when it should stop and ask you, and what it should hand back. For example:
   - *A workflow that fixes lint errors one file at a time and asks me before touching tests.*
   - *Plan a feature, let me approve the plan, build it task by task, and review each task.*
   - *Change my `bug-fix` workflow so a reviewer checks the fix before it finishes.*
4. Answer its questions. It asks only about what it cannot work out itself, such as inputs, hand-offs between steps, tools, what happens on failure, and the output.
5. Check its proposed design. Before writing anything it shows the pipeline with its loops, what each step does, is given and hands on, and the risks it sees. Change what you want, or agree. For a small, clearly described change it may go straight to saving.
6. When it reports the workflow as saved, select it in the **Mode** menu and run it. Its report says what to watch in the first run. Workflow Author never runs what it builds.

sections.heading: Workflow Author skill: how it designs a workflow
sections.text:
- **Starts from what you have.** It lists the workflows and profiles your workspace can use, including the built-in ones, and reads the ones it builds on, so a new workflow reuses the shapes and [profiles](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/behaviors/) that already work. It prefers profiles with the fewest permissions the step needs.
- **Knows the engine.** It builds with input, agent, verify (a gate), approval, subflow and output steps. That covers plan approval, a reviewer gate that sends only failures back, a plan of many tasks built one by one with a review each, and subflows that run another workflow or a single step in the middle of a flow. When unsure, it reads [How workflows work](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/how-workflows-work/) rather than guessing.
- **Designs for the models that run it.** Workflows are run by small and medium models that follow instructions literally. The author gives each step one job, splits multi-file work into a plan and a [task queue](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/how-workflows-work/#task-queues), never lets a step judge its own work, and makes every check need evidence. It keeps builders and reviewers within their task, keeps loops limited, binds each step only what it needs, and puts irreversible actions such as a push or a deploy late, behind an approval. It tells you when a shape you ask for is likely to fail, and why.
- **Writes full step instructions.** Each step is told its place in the workflow, what it is given, what to do, what to hand on and who checks it.
- **Can add profiles.** When no existing profile fits a step, it can save a new one with the workflow.

sections.heading: Workflow Author skill: review a workflow, or fix one that ran badly
sections.text:
Ask the author to review a workflow, for example *review my release workflow*. It reads it and lists problems, most serious first, each with the change it would make. Examples: a step doing too many jobs, a check that passes without evidence, a loop without a limit, a step that ignores your notes, or a push before anything is verified. It changes nothing until you agree.

When a run went wrong, describe what happened, for example *Build and Verify kept bouncing until it failed* or *the reviewer keeps asking for extra work*. Say which workflow it was and at which step. The author traces the symptom to a likely cause in the design and proposes the change.

sections.heading: Workflow Author skill: saving and revising workflows
sections.text:
Workflow Author saves with its own **save_workflow** tool, not with ordinary file or shell tools. It writes only `.rusty/workflows/<id>.json` and any new profiles in `.rusty/profiles/`.

- **Every save is validated first.** The whole graph and any new profiles are checked, including that every profile a step names exists among the built-in and workspace profiles. If anything is wrong, nothing is written. The author gets a list of issues, fixes them, and submits the complete workflow again.
- **Saves are all or nothing.** The workflow and its profiles are written together. If writing fails partway, files are put back as they were. The Agent and Behaviors lists refresh after a save.
- **Revisions keep what you didn't ask to change.** To revise, name the workflow. The author reads its current definition, changes only what you asked for, and resubmits the whole workflow. If the file changed in the meantime, for example because you edited it in the Workflow Editor, the save is refused so nothing is overwritten. The author reads it again and redoes the change.
- **Built-in workflows are not changed.** Asked to change one, it saves a changed copy under a new id, which you can then select instead.

**Saved is not the same as working.** A saved workflow is structurally valid, but that does not mean your provider is available, permissions are granted, or a run will succeed. Run it once and check the result. If a save fails, the author says so and shows the issues; it never reports a failed save as done.

Workflow Author can save only from a **Single agent** chat that is not in Plan or VFS mode and is not following a workflow. In Plan or VFS mode it can still read workflows and profiles. Workspace-created skills cannot save workflows. **build** stays the default skill for new chats.

sections.heading: Create a skill
sections.text:
1. Open **Skills** in the left rail.
2. Click **New Skill**.
3. Fill in:
   - a **name**,
   - a short description of **what this skill does**,
   - the **system prompt**, which is the instructions the model receives,
   - optionally a **model**. Leave it on **Use default model** to follow whatever model the chat uses.
4. Save. Rusty confirms with **Changes have been saved**.

Skills are saved per workspace as JSON files in `.rusty/skills/`, one file per skill, so you can commit them with your project. See [The .rusty folder](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/rusty-folder/).

sections.heading: Use a skill
sections.text: - In **Agent Mode**, choose a skill in the **Select skill** menu next to the message box. While the chat follows a [workflow](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/behaviors/), the menu stays on **build** and reads *tools set per step*: each step's profile decides its tools, and your choice returns with **Single agent**.

sections.heading: Skills or profiles?
sections.text:
They work at different levels:

- A **skill** is what you pick for a chat: the working style and prompt.
- A **profile** is used by a workflow step and controls tools, limits, rules and completion checks. Rusty ships [12 built-in profiles](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/built-in-workflows/#built-in-profiles).

See [Profiles & workflows](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/behaviors/) for profiles.

title: Smart tools & web search
summary: Let a cheaper model read whole files and pages, and hand your main model only the parts that matter.

sections.text:
**Smart tools are for the model, not for you.** They are the tools the agent itself calls to read files, search code and read web pages. When they are on, the work of reading is done by a *separate* model, the **selector**, and only the relevant parts go back to the model running your task, the **executing model**.

That has two effects:

- **Richer, more focused context.** The selector reads the whole file or page and picks out what answers the agent's question, so the executing model works from curated context instead of bulk.
- **Lower cost.** Reading a large amount of text is billed at the selector's price. If you pick a cheaper model with a long context window, you avoid paying your most expensive model to ingest text it mostly does not need.

All of the settings live under **Settings → Intelligence**.

sections.heading: How they work
sections.text:
1. The executing model calls an ordinary tool such as `read_file`, and describes precisely what it needs in a `request`.
2. Rusty gives the selector model the material: the whole file, the whole page, or the search request.
3. The selector picks out what is relevant.
4. Only that comes back to the executing model. If it is not enough, the agent asks again with a more specific request.

The agent sees these as normal tools with descriptions that tell it to be specific about what it needs, so there is nothing for you to invoke.

### The three smart tools

| Tool | What the selector does | What the executing model receives |
|------|------------------------|-----------------------------------|
| **Smart file reading** (`read_file`) | Reads the whole file and chooses the line ranges that answer the request. | Those exact lines as excerpts, not the complete file. |
| **Smart code search** (`search_codebase`) | Turns the described need into search patterns, which Rusty runs over the workspace. | A ranked, size-limited list of matching lines as file paths and line numbers, for follow-up reads. |
| **Smart web extraction** (`web_extract`) | Reads the fetched page and chooses the line ranges that answer the request. | Verbatim excerpts with the source URL and section headings. The full-page `web_fetch` tool stays available. |

The result is always the real text, ranked or excerpted. It is not a rewritten summary.

Smart tools work in Agent chats.

sections.heading: Turn one on
sections.text:
Each tool is off until you enable it.

1. Open **Settings → Intelligence** and find the tool's card: **Smart file reading**, **Smart code search** or **Smart web extraction**.
2. Choose a **Selector provider** and a **Selector model**.
3. Switch the tool on.

If no provider or model is available yet, the card asks you to choose one first.

> [!NOTE]
> The selector configuration is captured when a run starts and holds until that run finishes. Changing it in Settings affects the next run, not the one in progress.

sections.heading: Choosing the selector model
sections.text:
The selector is separate from the executing model, so you can make different trade-offs for each:

- **Cheaper than your executing model.** That is where the saving comes from.
- **A large context window.** The selector is shown the whole file or page, so more room means fewer cut-offs.
- **Reliable structured output.** The selector is asked to reply with a small JSON answer (line ranges, or search patterns). A model that follows that format consistently works best, and a reply that is not valid JSON makes the tool call fail.

Any model from any connected provider works. See [Model providers](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/providers/).

sections.heading: Limits
sections.text:
Smart tools keep results bounded so the executing model's context stays small.

| Tool | Limit |
|------|-------|
| `read_file` | The selector is shown up to about 180,000 characters of the file, and content beyond that is not visible to it. Up to 16 excerpts and 400 lines in total come back. |
| `web_extract` | The selector is shown up to about 180,000 characters of the page. Up to 12 excerpts, 300 lines and about 16,000 characters come back. |
| `search_codebase` | Up to 6 search patterns, and at most 5 matches per file. Output is capped at about 12,000 characters. |

The limits may change between releases.

sections.heading: Cost and observability
sections.text: Every smart-tool call is recorded in Tool Execution Observability as run by the selector model, along with its provider and a purpose: *Smart Read selector*, *Smart Search selector* or *Web Extract selector*. The tokens the selector spends are tracked separately from the executing model's own, so you can see exactly what the curation cost. See [Observability & metrics](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/observability/).

sections.heading: Web search providers
sections.text:
The agent's `web_search` tool needs a search provider. This is a separate setting from smart tools. Under **Settings → Intelligence → Web search providers**, add an API key for one or more:

| Provider | Notes |
|----------|-------|
| **OpenAI** | Uses the Responses API's built-in `web_search` tool. |
| **Brave Search** | |
| **Tavily** | |
| **Exa** | Works with no key through Exa's public MCP endpoint. |
| **Parallel** | |
| **Perplexity** | |
| **Gemini** | |

Each row has a **Get a key** link to that provider's key page. The first provider in the list with a configured key is used, in the order shown. Exa needs no key at all, so web search can work without any setup.

Keys are stored encrypted, the same way as your model provider keys. See [Data, storage & privacy](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/privacy/).

title: Source control
summary: Review agent changes, stage and commit, manage branches and browse history, all inside the IDE.

sections.text:
Git is the final checkpoint for everything an agent does, so Rusty has it built in. Open **Source Control** from the left rail. The icon shows a badge with the number of changed files, counting staged and unstaged changes across every repository in the workspace.

> [!NOTE]
> Source Control needs a folder to be open first. If you see *Open a folder first to view Source Control*, use **Open Workspace**.

sections.heading: Repositories
sections.text: A workspace can contain more than one repository, for example submodules or worktrees. Use the **Select repository** menu at the top to switch between them. Each repository has its own status, branch and history. For submodules there are actions to register one locally without cloning it, and to sync its local URL from `.gitmodules`.

sections.heading: Review and stage changes
sections.text:
The change list separates **staged** and **unstaged** changes. Open a file's diff to see exactly what changed, including what an agent just wrote. Right-click a change for more options, such as **Add to Git** and **Add to .gitignore**.

In the file tree, files show their Git state so you can see at a glance what has changed.

sections.heading: Commit
sections.text: Type a message in the commit box and press <kbd>⌘</kbd> <kbd>Enter</kbd> to commit.

sections.heading: Branches
sections.text:
The branch manager lets you:

- create a branch with **New Branch**,
- switch with **Checkout**,
- combine work with **Merge into Current**, and
- replay your work with **Rebase Current onto Selected**.

If a merge or rebase stops partway, use **Abort Merge/Rebase** to back out.

sections.heading: History
sections.text:
- Open the **commit graph** from the Source Control header to see how branches relate.
- The history list shows past commits for the repository.
- From any file, use **Open Git History of this File** to see just that file's commits.

sections.heading: Blame
sections.text: In the editor, use the blame toggle in the file toolbar, or click the line numbers, to see who last changed each line. Use **Reveal in File Tree** to jump from a file back to its place in the explorer.

sections.heading: A good habit
sections.text: Treat every agent run the way you would a colleague's pull request: read the diff before you commit.

title: Spec-driven development
summary: Write a spec, plan it, build it and keep it true, with every step saved as Markdown in your repository.

sections.text:
**Spec-driven development** makes the spec the unit of work. A change starts as Markdown in your repository and moves through four steps (specify, design and plan, implement, archive). Every step leaves files behind, so you, your team and any other coding agent can pick the work up from the folder alone.

It is built from two ideas. From [OpenSpec](https://github.com/Fission-AI/OpenSpec): a living description of what the system does, one spec per *capability*, which finished changes are merged into. From [GitHub Spec Kit](https://github.com/github/spec-kit): one folder per change, with a document for each concern and for each task. Rusty does not need either tool, and can [import](#importing) their folders and [export](#exporting) to either.

You find it on the **Specs** page of the **Documentation** tab. It reads plain files, so it works before the repository is analyzed.

sections.heading: The folder
sections.text:
Specs live in `specs/` at the root of the repository. They are meant to be committed.

```text
specs/
├── README.md                        the conventions, for people and other agents
├── project.md                       purpose, stack, commands, conventions, principles
├── capabilities/
│   └── albums/spec.md               what the system does now, as named requirements
├── changes/
│   └── 0007-photo-albums/
│       ├── change.md                status and history
│       ├── spec.md                  why, requirements with criteria, open questions
│       ├── checklist.md             quality questions about the spec, ticked when it answers them
│       ├── research.md              optional
│       ├── design.md                approach, files, data, risks
│       ├── tasks.md                 the ordered checklist
│       ├── tasks/T2-sidebar.md      one document per finished task
│       └── verification.md          every criterion, with its result
└── archive/
    └── 2026-10-30-0007-photo-albums/   finished changes, merged into capabilities
```

If `specs/` is already used for something else, put `{"root": "docs/specs"}` in `.rusty/specs.json` and Rusty uses that folder instead.

sections.heading: Set up
sections.text:
Open the **Specs** page. In a repository without specs you can:

- **Onboard this project.** For a project that already exists. See [Onboarding an existing project](#onboarding-an-existing-project).
- **Set up specs.** Writes `README.md` and a `project.md` template, without a model.
- **New change.** Creates the first change straight away.

The project file ends in a **Principles** section: the few, testable rules every change is checked against.

### Onboarding an existing project

A blank project can start with a change. A project that is already under way needs its current behavior written down first, so later changes have something to change. Onboarding does that in two steps, with you in between.

1. **Survey.** **Onboard this project** opens an Agent tab with the **Survey the project** workflow. Add what you know in the `Notes:` line (for a project with little code, describe what it is for) and send. Rusty reads the repository and writes `specs/project.md` and `specs/onboarding.md`, a list of the capabilities it found:

   ```markdown
   ## albums
   Purpose: grouping photos without moving them.
   Paths: `src/albums/`, `src/ui/AlbumSidebar.tsx`
   Notes: renaming is the tricky part
   ```

2. **Review the list.** Nothing else has been written yet. Open `onboarding.md` (**Edit onboarding.md** on the Project page) and rename, remove or add capabilities, or change the paths each one is read from. A capability's name becomes its folder under `capabilities/`.

3. **Write the specs.** The Project page shows the list with what is written and what is not. **Write spec** writes one capability's spec in its own run, reading the code at its paths and its tests, and leaves the message for you to send. **Write all remaining** starts the missing ones one after another in a single Agent tab without waiting for you; a run that fails or that you stop ends the batch. Each spec is a set of named requirements with *WHEN … THEN* scenarios, and is checked for [drift](#warnings).

Running the survey again keeps the entries you edited and revises the rest. **Rewrite** on a capability revises its spec and keeps what you wrote.

sections.heading: A change, step by step
sections.text:
### 1. New change

**New change** asks for a title and a sentence on why. It creates the next numbered folder with `change.md` and a `spec.md` template.

By default it also **creates and switches to a Git branch** named `spec/0007-photo-albums`, before writing the files, so the spec lands on the branch. Clear the checkbox to stay on your current branch. Outside a Git repository, in a repository with no commits, or when the branch name is taken, the change is still created and a notification says why there is no branch. Uncommitted work comes along to the new branch.

### 2. Specify

**Specify** opens an Agent tab with the **Specify a change** workflow. Its message is filled in with a `Notes:` line where you can add what you know. When you send it, Rusty reads the project file, the existing capabilities and the code, and writes `spec.md`:

```markdown
### R1: Albums can be created and named
Capability: albums (adds "Album creation")
A user creates an album with a name that is unique in the library.

- C1: WHEN the user creates an album with a new name THEN it appears in the sidebar.
- C2: WHEN the name is already taken THEN nothing is created and the reason is shown.
```

Before the spec is written, a **Clarify** step settles what the code can answer, records the defaults it takes under **Assumptions**, and keeps the few questions that change scope, security or what a user sees. Requirements state behavior, never the implementation, and each criterion has a result someone can check. User stories are ordered by priority (`US1 (P1)`), each with an independent check. **Success criteria** (`S1`) give measurable outcomes without naming any technology, and **Key entities** describe the data when there is some.

Requirements and criteria have ids (`R1`, `C1`) that tasks and verification refer to. Questions only you can answer are listed under **Open questions**, at most five, each with a recommended answer. Edit the file, or run Specify again with notes: it revises the current spec, keeps your edits and ids, and moves answered questions to **Clarifications**.

The `Capability:` line says what the requirement does to a capability once the change is finished: `adds`, `changes` or `removes` a named requirement.

The last step, **Checklist**, tests the spec the way unit tests test code and writes `checklist.md`. It asks questions about the writing, not the software, such as *Are the limits on an album name specified?*, grouped by completeness, clarity, consistency, measurability, scenario and edge coverage, non-functional needs, dependencies and scope. It adds a section for the domain the change is about, such as user experience, an interface, security or data. Each item (`CHK001`) points to the part of the spec it is about, or is marked `[Gap]`, `[Ambiguity]`, `[Conflict]` or `[Assumption]`. Items the spec answers are ticked. Open items say what is missing, and the Specs page counts them (a warning once the change is planned). Design & tasks reads them as gaps to handle or name. Untick an item you disagree with. Close an open item by editing the spec or running Specify again, which re-answers the checklist and keeps your ticks and its ids.

### 3. Design & tasks

**Design & tasks** writes `design.md` (approach, files and symbols, data and contracts, failure handling, tests, and a check against the project's principles) and then `tasks.md`:

```markdown
- [ ] **T1** Album model and storage. R1 (C1, C2)
  Add `Album` to `src/albums/model.rs` and persist it with the library.
- [ ] **T2** Create and rename albums from the sidebar. R1 (C1) after T1
```

Between the design and the tasks, a **Check** step compares spec and design: every criterion needs a part of the design and a test, and gaps and conflicts are rated before the tasks are written. Tasks are grouped in phases: setup, foundation, one phase per user story in priority order (the first is the MVP), and a final check. Each phase has a checkpoint saying what can be tried once it is done. Each task names the requirements and criteria it satisfies and the tasks it comes after, and every criterion is named by at least one task. A range such as `C1–C3` or `after T1–T3` names every id in it. The Tasks step cannot finish while a criterion is named by no task, a task names no criterion or an id that is not in the spec, or the `after` links form a circle: the list goes back to it with what to fix before `tasks.md` is written. Both files are yours to edit before anything is built. Ticking a task by hand marks it done; unticking it reopens it.

Specify and Design & tasks write straight into the folder. There is no approval step: read the files (and the branch's diff), edit them, or run the step again with notes.

### 4. Implement

**Implement** builds the tasks that are not ticked yet, one at a time. Each task gets a step plan, a fresh builder and a review against the criteria it names. Then **Verify** checks *every* criterion of the spec, not just those of this run's tasks, and you try the checks only a person can do. This is the [task queue](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/how-workflows-work/) of the other workflows, with the folder as the plan.

What it leaves in the change folder, also when a run fails or you stop it:

- the tasks it finished, ticked in `tasks.md`;
- `tasks/T2-<title>.md` for each, with what was built and how it was reviewed;
- `verification.md`, with every criterion and its result;
- the status in `change.md`: `building`, then `verifying` once every task is ticked, then `done` when verification and your manual checks pass.

A run starts from the files, so a stopped run continues after the tasks it finished. If every task is already ticked, a single *final check* task confirms the whole spec against the code and fixes what is missing. Ticks are written when the run ends, not as each task finishes; if the app crashes mid-run, that run's progress is lost.

### 5. Archive

**Archive** merges a finished change into the capability specs and moves the folder to `specs/archive/<date>-<folder>/`.

- A requirement that **adds** appears in its capability with its criteria as scenarios; one that **changes** replaces the requirement of that name in place; one that **removes** deletes it. A capability that does not exist yet is created.
- If a merge is impossible (adding a name that exists, changing or removing one that does not), nothing is written and the message says which requirement.
- Requirements without a `Capability:` line are merged nowhere and reported.
- The change must be `done` with every task ticked. Otherwise Rusty asks, and **Archive anyway** archives it as it is.

sections.heading: Changes across several repositories
sections.text:
When the workspace holds several repositories, one change can span some of them, for example a backend, an app and the website.

1. Open the repository that should hold the **main spec** in the repository picker, and choose **New change**. The dialog lists the workspace's other repositories. Tick the ones the change also touches.
2. Rusty creates one change folder in each repository, each numbered in its own repository. They all switch to one branch named after the main part, such as `spec/0004-dark-mode`. Each `change.md` names the repository with the main spec (`main:`) and the other parts (`links: [rusty-core/0002-dark-mode]`).
3. Run **Specify** in the main repository first. It writes the spec of the whole change and marks each requirement with the repository that delivers it (`Repository: rusty-core`). What two repositories exchange, such as an API, a file format or an event, gets its own requirement that names both.
4. Then open each other part (**Open** in the change's *This change spans …* box) and run **Specify** there. Each part writes only its repository's share, pointing back to the main requirement it comes from.
5. **Design & tasks** and **Implement** run per part. Each step is shown the other parts' state and their designs, so the contracts stay the same, and it builds only in its own repository. A task that needs another part's work first says so, for example *Needs rusty-core T3 first*. Run the parts in that order.
6. **Switch all to `spec/…`** in the same box puts every part's repository on the change's branch. Uncommitted work in a repository is stashed for the branch it was on and comes back when you return to that branch, as with Rusty's branch menu.

The steps run in the workspace folder, so their messages name paths from there (`rusty-ide/specs/changes/…`). Each part is archived in its own repository.

sections.heading: Your own step instructions
sections.text: Each step has detailed built-in instructions. To add your team's rules, create `specs/instructions/<step>.md`, where `<step>` is `specify`, `plan`, `implement`, `start` or `capability`. Its text is added to that step's context after the documents, and `specs/instructions/all.md` is added to every step. For example, `plan.md` could say "Every design needs a Rollback section" or "Write decisions as short ADRs". The files are read when the run starts, so a change applies to the next run.

sections.heading: Statuses
sections.text:
| Status | Means |
|--------|-------|
| `draft` | The folder exists; the spec is not written. |
| `specified` | A spec exists. |
| `planned` | `tasks.md` exists. |
| `building` | Some tasks are ticked. |
| `verifying` | Every task is ticked; verification has not passed. |
| `done` | Verification and the manual checks passed. |
| `archived` | Merged into the capabilities and moved. |

The status is a record, not a lock. The page also shows what the files say: if every task is ticked while the status is `planned`, it tells you and never rewrites the status itself. A folder written by hand, without `change.md`, gets a status from the documents it holds.

sections.heading: Warnings
Using the specs in chats
sections.text:
- **Use in chats.** On a change, this marks it as the one you are working on. Chats and agents are then told about it: its title, status, progress, its open tasks and where its files are. The choice is remembered for the repository.
- **`spec_context`.** A read-only tool every agent and workflow step can use. With no input it lists the project, the capabilities and the changes with their status and next step. With `change` (the folder name, the number, or part of the title) it returns that change's open tasks and the documents asked for (`spec`, `design`, `tasks`, `research`, `verification`; spec and design by default). Like `repo_context`, it is granted along with `read_file`. See [Profiles & workflows](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/behaviors/).

sections.heading: Importing and exporting
sections.text:
### Importing

If the repository already has an `openspec/` folder or Spec Kit's `.specify/` and `specs/001-feature/` folders, the Specs page offers **Import from OpenSpec** or **Import from Spec Kit**. It is a one-time, non-destructive copy: the original stays where it is, nothing that already exists in `specs/` is overwritten, and a change that was imported before is skipped.

| From OpenSpec | Becomes |
|---------------|---------|
| `project.md` | `project.md`, with a Principles section added if it had none |
| `specs/<capability>/spec.md` | `capabilities/<capability>/spec.md`; the `## Purpose` section becomes the `Purpose:` line |
| `changes/<name>/proposal.md` and its `ADDED`, `MODIFIED` and `REMOVED` delta specs | a numbered change: Why and What changes from the proposal, one requirement per delta with a `Capability:` line, each scenario as a criterion |
| `design.md`, `tasks.md` | `design.md`; `tasks.md` renumbered `T1`, `T2`, … with ticks kept and the group as instructions |
| `changes/archive/` | not imported |

| From Spec Kit | Becomes |
|---------------|---------|
| `.specify/memory/constitution.md` | the Principles of `project.md` |
| `specs/001-feature/spec.md` | `spec.md`: one requirement per user story with its Given/When/Then scenarios as criteria, one for the functional requirements, `[NEEDS CLARIFICATION]` markers as open questions |
| `plan.md`, `research.md` | `design.md`, `research.md` |
| `checklists/*.md` | one `checklist.md`, a section per checklist, ticks kept |
| `tasks.md` | renumbered `T1`, `T2`, … with ticks kept and the phase as instructions |
| `data-model.md`, `quickstart.md`, `contracts/` | stay where they are, listed at the end of `design.md` |

Imported tasks do not name requirements or criteria, so the page shows warnings that criteria are not named by any task; add the references or ignore them. The conversions are best effort.

### Exporting

Your specs stay the source. On the **Project** page, **Export to OpenSpec** and **Export to Spec Kit** write them in the other tool's layout, so a team that works there can use them. It is a one-way, non-destructive copy: nothing that already exists in the target is overwritten (it is listed as left alone), and each exported change gets a line in its history, so importing from that folder later does not bring it back as a second copy. Run it again after more changes to add the new ones; changes already exported are not updated.

| To OpenSpec | Written as |
|-------------|------------|
| `project.md` | `openspec/project.md` |
| `capabilities/<name>/spec.md` | `openspec/specs/<name>/spec.md`, with a `## Purpose` section and each criterion as a `#### Scenario:` with **WHEN**, **THEN** and **AND** lines |
| each change, active or archived | `openspec/changes/<slug>/` (archived: `changes/archive/<date>-<slug>/`) with `proposal.md` (Why, What Changes, Impact), `design.md`, `tasks.md` and a delta spec per capability: requirements that **add** go under `ADDED`, **change** under `MODIFIED`, **remove** under `REMOVED` |

Requirements without a `Capability:` line belong to no capability and are not written to OpenSpec.

| To Spec Kit | Written as |
|-------------|------------|
| the Principles of `project.md` | `.specify/memory/constitution.md` |
| each change | `specs/NNN-slug/` with `spec.md` (one user story per requirement, its criteria as Given/When/Then, a functional requirement for each, open questions as `[NEEDS CLARIFICATION]`), `plan.md` (the design), `research.md`, `checklists/requirements.md` (the checklist) and `tasks.md` (`T001`, `T002`, … with ticks kept) |

Capability specs have no Spec Kit equivalent and are not exported to it. The conversions are best effort, and checked by exporting and importing back, not against the tools themselves.

sections.heading: Good to know
sections.text:
- The workflows are [built-in workflows](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/built-in-workflows/#spec-workflows), so you can pick the models they use like any other, and Auto never starts them on its own.
- Specify, Design & tasks and Implement run in the workspace folder. The repository must be that folder or one inside it. The Specs page itself works for any repository you pick.
- A step's documents are written when its run finishes. Stopping Specify or Design & tasks saves nothing.
- Running Specify or Design & tasks again replaces the file with a revision of the current text. Git keeps the previous version.

title: Supported languages & frameworks
summary: Which languages, infrastructure files and frameworks repository analysis reads, and what it reads for each.

sections.text: [Repository analysis](https://rusty-edit.dev/docs/repository-analysis/) reads source files and project files without running or building anything. How much it can tell you depends on the language: every language below gets the import graph, the Architecture tab, the Files map and code health scores. Infrastructure files (Terraform, pipelines, Dockerfiles and more) are scored too, [below](#infrastructure-and-devops-files). Files in other languages still count in the totals, but are not connected in the graph.

sections.heading: Languages
sections.text:
| Language | Files read | Project files read | Code health |
|----------|------------|--------------------|:---:|
| Rust | `.rs` | `Cargo.toml` | Yes |
| TypeScript | `.ts`, `.tsx`, `.mts`, `.cts` | `package.json`, `tsconfig.json` | Yes |
| JavaScript | `.js`, `.jsx`, `.mjs`, `.cjs` | `package.json` | Yes |
| Python | `.py` | `pyproject.toml`, `setup.py`, `setup.cfg`, `requirements.txt` | Yes |
| Java | `.java` | `pom.xml`, `build.gradle` | Yes |
| Kotlin | `.kt`, `.kts` | `build.gradle.kts` | Yes |
| Go | `.go` | `go.mod` | Yes |
| C# | `.cs` | `.csproj` | Yes |
| PHP | `.php` | `composer.json` | Yes |
| C | `.c`, `.h` | `CMakeLists.txt`, `compile_commands.json` | Yes |
| C++ | `.cc`, `.cpp`, `.cxx`, `.hpp`, `.hh`, `.hxx` and similar | `CMakeLists.txt`, `compile_commands.json` | Yes |

Some notes on how imports are resolved:

- **Rust** imports are resolved to the item they name, including `#[path]` modules and re-exports.
- **TypeScript and JavaScript** follow `tsconfig.json` `paths`, `baseUrl` and `extends`, and resolve sibling workspace packages to their entry file. Each import is marked runtime or type-only, which is what the **Imports** filter in the Architecture tab uses.
- **Java and Kotlin** share one resolver, so imports between Kotlin and Java files in the same project are connected. `*.gradle.kts` files are treated as build files, not sources.
- **C and C++** connect `#include` directives to files, using include directories from `compile_commands.json` or `CMakeLists.txt` when present.

Code health scores need per-function measurements (complexity, nesting, parameters, class cohesion), which exist today for Rust, TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Java, Kotlin, Go, C#, PHP, C and C++ (C is measured with the C++ grammar). Go methods are grouped by their receiver type, since Go declares them outside the type. The Code health page lists the languages it measured and how many files are in other languages.

sections.heading: Infrastructure and DevOps files
sections.text:
Files that configure how software is built and run are scored on the Code health page too. They are not part of the import graph; Rusty finds them by name and content anywhere in the repository (skipping `.gitignore`d folders, `node_modules`, `.terraform` and similar).

| Kind | Files recognized | Examples of what is checked |
|------|------------------|-----------------------------|
| Terraform | `*.tf` | Unpinned providers and modules, variables without a type or description, unused variables, locals and data sources, provisioners, security groups open to `0.0.0.0/0`, hardcoded account ids, local module paths that do not exist |
| Terragrunt | `terragrunt.hcl`, `root.hcl`, `*.terragrunt.hcl` | Unpinned sources, dependency loops between units, dependencies on directories that are not units, deep include chains, missing remote state |
| GitHub Actions | `.github/workflows/*.yml`, composite `action.yml` | Actions not pinned to a commit, `write-all` permissions, untrusted event data in `run` scripts, `pull_request_target` checking out pull request code, missing timeouts, retired runners, `needs` loops and unknown jobs, references to local workflows that do not exist |
| GitLab CI, CircleCI, Azure Pipelines | `.gitlab-ci.yml`, `.circleci/config.yml`, `azure-pipelines*.yml` | Images without a fixed tag, unpinned includes and orbs, long inline scripts |
| Dockerfile | `Dockerfile`, `Dockerfile.*`, `*.dockerfile`, `Containerfile` | Floating base images, running as root, `ADD` instead of `COPY`, apt caches left in layers, secrets in `ENV`, copy-everything-before-install |
| Docker Compose | `docker-compose*.yml`, `compose.y*ml` | Floating images, privileged services and host networking, `depends_on` loops |
| Kubernetes | YAML with `apiVersion` and `kind` | Floating image tags, privileged containers, missing resource limits and probes |
| Ansible | playbooks and role task files | Tasks without names, shell and command tasks that always report a change |
| Shell | `*.sh`, `*.bash`, files with a shell shebang | No `set -euo pipefail`, downloads piped into a shell, unquoted variables |
| Makefile | `Makefile`, `*.mk` | Command targets missing from `.PHONY`, targets defined twice |
| Repository files | `.gitignore`, `CODEOWNERS`, `.env`, `*.tfstate`, private keys | Missing ignore patterns, CODEOWNERS rules that match no file, committed state files, environment files and keys |

Secrets written as literals in pipeline variables, Compose environments and similar places are reported for every kind above. Findings in these files come with the same fix prompts as code findings, and files with Git history also get the change-history findings (bug-fix commits, ownership, files changed together with many others).
